PRESENTATION OF THIRD REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the third report of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs. This report deals with the subject of misleading advertising and recommends major changes to the Competition Act such as the inclusion of a class action procedure and appropriate administrative remedies to ensure consumer redress for misleading advertising.
After hearing witnesses on this subject for several months and travelling to Washington to see how they deal with misleading advertising and deceptive marketing practices, your committee came to the conclusion that Canadian consumers should be better protected against those engaged in misleading advertising.
Our objective during the investigation was to find ways to improve the current system. We believe our recommendations do just that.

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure, indeed honour, to present pursuant to Standing Order 106 a petition on behalf of a number of constituents who are of the opinion that the Government lacks a mandate from the people of Canada to conclude a trade agreement. I suspect these people have actually read the agreement and have come to that conclusion, unlike the Minister.
They believe that the proposed trade deal would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and therefore undermine Canada's ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States. Since the trade deal failed to provide us with secure access to the U.S. market and threatens a loss of hundreds of thousands of Canadian jobs, they call upon Parliament to dissolve now and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade deal during a national general election.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-135, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff (code 9956), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to present to the House today Bill C-135, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff, for second reading. This Bill has being introduced in order to extend for a specified period the statutory authority which allows Canadian customs officials to prohibit the importation of obscene material and hate propaganda into Canada.
The Government is bringing in this Bill at this time because the authority provided under the Customs Tariff which prohibits the importation of hate propaganda, as well as obscene, seditious or treasonable materials, expires on June 30, 1988. This provision allows the Government to prevent the importation of the most virulent forms of violent, degrading and dehumanizing materials such as child pornography, depictions of violence against women, and many other things which are so repugnant to Canadians.
As Members of the House will recall, a sunset clause was initially inserted under this authority in 1985 in anticipation of new legislation on pornography which was to include amendments to the Criminal Code. The original sunset clause has since been amended on two separate occasions in order to extend the prohibition authority while the proposed pornography legislation was under consideration by Parliament.
While the provisions of Bill C-54 may be a matter of some debate, I do not believe that any Member of this House would want pornographic materials to enter the Canadian market unrestricted. I believe that as Members of Parliament we owe it to the Canadian public to ensure that such materials continue to be prohibited from entry.
Therefore I urge all Members to join with me this morning in giving unanimous and speedy approval to this technical amendment to extend the period of effect of this provision until December 31, 1989 and thereby ensure that there will be no lapse in the prohibition on the importation of obscene material and hate propaganda. The content is not changed. We are staying with the status quo. All we are doing with this Bill is extending the deadline for 18 months to December, 1989.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to make a few comments on Bill C-135, which amends the Customs Tariff by extending the period during which a definition of pronography may be used by customs officers to stop at our borders pornographic material that someone is trying to bring into Canada.
June 28, 1988

Unfortunately matters are not quite as simple as the Minister who has just spoken would have us believe. The Minister is bringing before the House Bill C-135, which at first sight is designed simply to extend the definition for this tariff code for one year.
However, things are a little more complicated than that, and Bill C-135, which is being brought in by the governement, is intended not merely to extend the tariff code but also to conceal the government's failure to bring before the House a real bill dealing with pornography and hate literature.
This is not the first time the government has brought back to us a measure aimed at extending these provisions. To sketch in the background of the situation, Mr. Speaker,...

You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that under the Customs Tariff Act customs officials are empowered to forbid entry into Canada of material of an immoral or indecent character. The definition of what constituted obscene material under the Customs Tariff Act used to be broader than the definition of obscenity contained in Section 159(8) of the Criminal Code.
This did not pose a problem until March, 1985 when the Federal Court of Appeal found that the obscenity provisions of the Customs Tariff Act were so vague as to be an unreasonable limit on the freedom of expression guarantee contained in Section 2(b) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Therefore the court struck down these provisions and, until Parliament acted in April, 1985, there were no restrictions on the importation of obscene materials.
The Tory Government came into power and in April, 1985, instead of bringing in comprehensive legislation dealing not only with the entry into Canada and the dissemination within Canada but with the printing in Canada, the showing of obscene materials, and the dissemination of hate propaganda material, the Government decided to operate by way of a stopgap measure which at the time was known as Bill C-38. Bill C-38 in fact incorporated the obscenity and hate propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code into the Customs Tariff Act. I think the Minister will have to agree that this is what happened in April, 1985.
The problem is that Bill C-38 was introduced for only one year and it lapsed on June 13, 1986. In other words, during the course of that one year the Government did not find time to put together a comprehensive piece of legislation dealing with obscene material, with pornography, and with hate literature.
What did it do a year later since it had not found the time to do the proper thing? It brought before the House Bill C-111, as Your Honour may remember, because Your Honour is very assiduous in attending this House. Your Honour must remember that in June, 1986 Bill C-l 11 was brought in, which
Customs Tariff
Bill extended the application of these obscenity and propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code and the Customs Tariff Act until December 31, 1987.
However, after a second year the Government had not yet brought before the House and passed a proper piece of legislation, so what did it do? In December, 1987 it came forward with Bill C-87 to extend further the stop-gap measure by one year.
What is happening this year? The Government is bringing forward Bill C-135 to further extend the provisions by one year. The real reason for all these extensions is the failure of the Government to pass new pornography legislation which would address the definition problems contained in both the Criminal Code and the Customs Tariff Act.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Government's new pornography legislation, Bill C-54, which I must admit it tried to pass through the House, did not wash. The legislation was decried. It was criticized by several elements in our society. It was depicted as backwards and Victorian. I also remember Members in this very House saying that it went much too far, that it would impose undue constraints even on libraries which would have to post signs stating that certain books contain material purported to be either obscene or pornographic because of an ill-advised piece of legislation, Bill C-54. In the opinion of some it would even criminalize normal adult sexual activity.

What happened is very simple: the government did not pass Bill C-54, it left it on the Order Paper. The government saw the country was against Bill C-5 and it didn't try to get it passed.
So today we have reached a point where the last extension of a definition of obscenity, of pornography, which allowed our customs officers to stop such material at the border, is running out, since Bill C-97, which was brought in last year, "expires" this week, on June 30, in two days, in other words, as it's already June 28.
The government, having failed to bring in a reasonable piece of legislation, containing definitions of pornography that would be acceptable in Canada (unlike Bill C-54, which was not acceptable to a majority of Canadians), now finds itself obliged once again to extend this provision for a year, to gain time. I don't wish to impute motives to the government, but this does give the impression that the government is trying to buy time so it can come before the people at the next election without really having tackled the problem of pornography in Canada, without having done its duty by bringing in legislation that would also cover hate literature.
This is what really lies behind Bill C-135, which at first sight is perfectly innocuous since it consists of exactly one line. I'll read it to you, Mr. Speaker, it's extremely simple. It has only the one clause, clause 1, which reads as follows:

June 28, 1988
Customs Tariff
Code 9956 in Schedule VII to the Customs Tariff is amended by striking
out the works following paragraph (d) thereof and substituting the following
therefor:
and I quote:
"(This code expires December 31,1989.)"
So all this mysterious language, which at first sight seems very simple, contitutes not just an extension of a customs tariff but a way for the Government to shirk its responsibilities and try to make it to the next elections without really having tackled the problem of pornography and hate literature in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable that the Government is putting off the admission that it made a mistake in presenting an unacceptable piece of legislation like Bill C-54, and putting off the drafting of another bill that would be more reasonable, more in line with the views of the majority of Canadians today, in the Canada we live in now. It is quite obvious that without an adequate bill defining appropriately what is obscene, what is pornographic, we don't have much choice but to vote for this extension of the customs tariff, so that at least unacceptable pornographic material doesn't get into Canada from other countries. But that doesn't really solve the problem of pornography, which can be home-grown. The government is evading its responsibilities.
It is thus with regret that we are going to support Bill C-135, but I wanted to review for you, Mr. Speaker, all the events that led up to this Bill, events the Government has no right to be proud of.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to represent my Party on Bill C-135 this morning. My remarks will not be long. I feel that this is an experience that we have endured-and I use the word advisedly-before, in regard to the extension of the expiry date of the Customs Tariff respecting the prohibition on the import of pornographic materials and hate literature. It is a rather sad irony that we are forced to do this again, for I believe the third time, and particularly that we are forced to do so because of a judgment of the Federal Court of Appeal.
That judgment, after all, ruled on the applicability of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I believe that when that Charter was passed most of us thought that it would be something that could be used to protect the weaker members of our society against the sort of aggression that the importation of pornography and hate literature represents.
By the perverse machinations of the legal system it came up with a ruling that rather made it easier to import pornography and hate literature into Canada. I think that it is a sad reflection on the way in which power has been vested in the judiciary in our society and taken away from the democratically elected organs of society that we are forced to do this now again, as I said, for the third time.
I should take this opportunity to point out to Canadians and to Members of the House the very narrow distinction, if any exists, between pornography and hate literature. We in this Party believe that much of what is today termed pornography is in fact hate literature aimed at women and children and that the function of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms should be to protect society, and thus women and children, from those forms of hate literature.
Because of the striking down of provision 99210 in the Customs Tariff which prohibited, and I quote, "the importation of books, printed paper, drawings, paintings, prints, photographs or representations of any kind of a treasonable or seditious or of an immoral or indecent character", we have amended the Customs Tariff. The other reason we are amending the Customs Tariff is of course the fact that we have not had a Bill passed in this House which defines and outlaws pornography and hate literature.
My hon. friend from Saint-Jacques pointed out that simply the importation was governed by the Customs Tariff and that there was no provision in Bill C-135 that would effectively control locally produced obscene or hate propaganda materials.
The Government has been successful to a limited degree by providing a tighter definition of obscene material in the Customs Tariff. I do not believe the insertion of a sunset clause was unwise, but it is because the sunset clause and its latest reincarnation expire this weekend that we have to come forward with this motion to extend that sunset clause for 18 months, and it has to be by means of a Bill.
I sincerely hope, and I am sure all Canadians share this sentiment whatever are their views on the matter of pornography and hate literature, that within 18 months either this Government or our Government which will succeed it, will manage to bring in a workable definition of pornography and hate literature that can be widely supported within the Canadian community and can be applied not only to prevent the importation of such materials but also to prevent their local production.
By the operation of Bill C-135, obscene material according to Section 159 and hate propaganda according to Section 281.3 of the Criminal Code, always assuming the perverse and capricious other House does not interfere with the passage thereof, will be prohibited from introduction into Canada for a further 18 months.
Let us not lose sight of the objective that we should have in this House, the objective of producing a workable definition of what is pornography, what is hate literature, what is erotica, and of enshrining that definition into law so that we can safeguard Canadians, particularly women and children, from the effects of what I believe can ultimately be included in the definition of hate propaganda.
June 28, 1988

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before going to Committee of the Whole, I would like to make a few comments at second reading, as I am entitled to do. I would also like to explain to my constituents and to those who are listening to us the reason for Bill C-135, An Act to amend the Customs Tariff (code 9956). This kind of thing is all Greek to a lot of people, and I would like to make sure that it's at least clear.
What the government is proposing, Mr. Speaker, is that the expiry date for the application of the Criminal Code to code 9956 of Schedule VII of the Customs Tariff be extended. It reads as follows:
Books, printed paper, drawings, paintings, prints, or representations of any kind which:
a) are deemed to be obscene within the meaning of section 159(8) of the Criminal Code.
You have to look at the Criminal Code to understand what that means, and section 159(8) of the Criminal Code reads as follows, Mr. Speaker:
(8) ["Obscene".] For the purposes of this Act, any publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex, or of sex and any one or more of the following subjects, namely crime, horror, cruelty and violence, shall be deemed to be obscene.
Mr. Speaker, section 9956 continues as follows:
(b)	constitute hate propaganda within the meaning of subsection 281.3(8) of the Criminal Code.
Section 281.3(1) of the Criminal Code reads as follows:
(Warrant of seizure) A judge who is satisfied by information upon oath that there are reasonable grounds for believing that any publication, copies of which are kept for sale or distribution in premises within the jurisdiction of the court is hate propaganda, shall issue a warrant under his hand authorizing seizure of the copies.
Thus it is possible for a judge to take action. I return to section 9956, and I quote:
(c)	are of a treasonable character within the meaning of section 46 of the Criminal Code.
Now, section 46 of the Criminal Code states:
46. Everyone commits high treason who, in Canada,
(a)	kills or attempts to kill Her Majesty,
(b)	levies war against Canada,
(c)	assists an enemy, etc.
It goes on at length, Mr. Speaker, but essentially it covers treason and other offences against the authority and person of the Queen.
Customs Tariff
(d)	are of a seditious character within the meaning of sections 60 and 61 of
the Criminal Code.
That is, persons who take part in an organized rebellion against public authority.
Sections 60 and 61 of the Criminal Code read as follows:
Sedition
(1)	Seditious words are words that express a seditious intention.
(2)	A seditious libel is a libel that expresses a seditious intention.
It explains what is meant by seditious words, libel, conspiracy and intention, and section 61 sets out a few exceptions.
Mr. Speaker, the government has introduced Bill C-135 in order to extend the life of the aforementioned sections because it does not have the courage to bring forward Bill C-54, which promised and proposed amendments that would provide Canadians with better legislation on pornography and hate literature.
Mr. Speaker, this is yet another sign of a government that is continually wavering, unable to make a firm decision and proceed with a bill it originated, devised and drafted itself, a government that is indecisive because it lacks courage.
Naturally, we will not oppose Bill C-135. I would like the government to know, however, that its lack of courage, its inability to act, to make decisions, to put firm legislation before the Canadian people, were discussed on television again yesterday.
I could recite the history of the bills that have languished in the House for a year or more. Already three bills have been passed to delay introducing provisions dealing with items that may be pornographic or seditious.

There was Bill C-38, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff Act. It received Royal Assent on April 13, 1985. At the time the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) argued that while the Liberal Party supported the Bill it was only a stop-gap measure. We said that in 1985. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal pressed for a response, in terms of legislation, to the Badgley and Fraser reports. I recommend Members read Hansard at pages 3604 to 3606 of April 2, 1985, wherein the Hon. Member for Mount Royal made a very good and thoughtful speech on the subject.
Later on, Bill C-lll further extended the code until December 31, 1987. It received Royal Assent on June 26, 1986. Again, I invite Members to read Hansard at page 14,306 to page 14,311. Still later, Bill C-87, an Act respecting the harmonized tariff system, received Royal Assent on December 17, 1987, and extended the code to June, 1988. Now, two days before the expiry of the code, government Members come into the House and say: "Hey, quickly pass this Bill, please, because we would like to act", and conserve or reserve, or pickle code 9956 of the Customs Tariff.

June 28, 1988
Customs Tariff
We only have a small number of MPs on this side. It will not be long. We do not mind telling the Government with its large numbers that if it decided to have it its way democracy would possibly be at work. They have to make decisions. They have to make up their minds what they want. They have Bill C-54 before the House, which indeed they probably will not call; they do not have the courage to call it.
As a lady said on TV last night, "if you don't like it, at least let us look at it to amend it or withdraw the darn thing and come in with something stronger, more in keeping with Canadian expectations". However, putting off and extending things is a sign of indecisiveness, a sign of those who do not know what they want, a sign of those who should not be governing the country.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we certainly support the amendment coming back from the Senate on Bill C-115. 1 want to take this opportunity to say that this was a result of co-operation by a large number of people representing different levels of government, the Minister, his associates, the opposition Parties, and the initiative, I might say, of the Kamloops Indian Band. He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to put before you for second reading today Bill C-137 to establish the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program. At this point I would like to thank the Opposition for agreeing to deal with this matter expeditiously because it is an important program for Canada.

The program I announced on May 3 will be of great importance to the petroleum and mining exploration sectors of the Canadian economy. In that sense, the program has a specific target, but from a broader standpoint, it will have more widespread significance since all Canadians benefit, in the long run, from higher profits earned by any industry.

The oil and gas industry employs many thousands of Canadians directly and indirectly. When we include the oil and the gas downstream and the metal fabrication components, we are really talking about one-quarter of a million direct jobs and many more thousands of indirect jobs for Canadians.
The purpose of this Bill is very simple. It is to provide an opportunity for junior exploration companies to maintain an adequate level of exploration financing by raising new equity through the use of flow-through shares. In this way they can continue to contribute to our economic objectives and to the type of country we hope to share into the 1990s and beyond. The program will provide a positive environment in which our exploration industries are free to do what they do best, namely, explore for, develop, and market Canada's mineral and hydrocarbon wealth.
My colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), retained the flow-through share mechanism in the tax reform package which he introduced last year. We in the Government know that flow-through shares work. They provide funds efficiently for exploration and they have brought prosperity to many of the outlying regions of Canada. Even before tax reform the Government moved on a number of occasions since 1984 to improve flow-through share financing. We extended the period of eligibility so that expenses made in January and February could be claimed for taxation purposes for the previous year. The flow-through share mechanism was thus more responsive to the realities of winter drilling. With tax reform we also lowered taxes for the mining industry in line with general rate reduction, and the industry as a whole has started to do very well.

June 28, 1988
Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act
However, with the unforeseen downturn in the stock market on October 19, economic conditions changed all equity markets including the market for exploration issues. Funds became more difficult to raise. This, combined with the planned phasing out of the Mining Exploration Depletion Allowance or MEDA over the next few years, gave us cause for concern. If I had to capsulize what this program is all about, I would say that it will bring sustained and ongoing growth for the mining and oil and gas industries.
CEIP, the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program, will provide an estimated $210 million per year to these resource exploration sectors so that junior exploration companies, be they looking for oil and gas or minerals, will be able to maintain an adequate level of financing or exploration. This translates into about $700 million annually for exploration activity for projects which go ahead as a result of this program. It can be expected to generate about 12,000 person-years of employment. As Hon. Members of the House realize, most of those jobs will be in areas of Canada where we desperately need new job creation. The program will begin on January 1, 1989 for mining companies. For the oil and gas industry, the program will kick in on October 1, 1988. The different commencement dates stem from the different phase out schedules for MEDA and the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program on the energy or hydrocarbons side.
Eligible companies will be able to claim 30 per cent of their eligible exploration expenses, up to a maximum of $10 million in expenses per company per year. This is a direct incentive payment. It is not within the tax system. After all, a fundamental principle of a responsible Government is that public expenditures are not hidden in the tax system if at all possible. Otherwise we would lose the fiscal responsibility which the Government promotes because we believe that Canadians have a right to know how their money is being spent.
Let me say a word about the $10 million ceiling per company. We can target the money to smaller companies by placing a cap on individual claims. It is a fairly generous cap including a 30 per cent payment which would limit an applicant to receiving 30 per cent of a maximum of $10 million, or about $3 million a year. This meets the requirements of most exploration programs for junior exploration companies.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we have planned to phase out the Mining Exploration Depletion Allowance over the next few years. The 30 per cent under CEIP is somewhat more generous than the previous depletion incentive, but we felt that this was warranted by current market conditions and as a result of what happened to the equity markets since October 19.
However, to allow us time to consult with industry and to implement this program, the Minister of Finance agreed in his announcement of May 3, 1988 to extend MEDA for individuals to the end of this year, December 31, 1988, at a full rate of 33 and one-third per cent. This will allow us time for a smooth
transition from MEDA to our new program, CEIP. The industry likes the particular arrangement very well. The 30 per cent rate will be guaranteed for two years until the end of 1990, after which it may be adjusted up or down according to market conditions and how much incentive is required to maintain healthy levels of exploration.
Mineral exploration expenses that will be eligible for CEIP include those incurred on primary or grass roots exploration by qualified companies financed through issuing flow-through shares. Those expenses are the ones that currently qualify for the Mining Exploration Depletion Allowance which can be flowed through to the investors. In the oil and gas sectors expenses which are purely exploratory in nature and financed by means of flow-through shares are eligible. CEIP will strengthen the flow-through share concept. Exploration companies or limited partnerships acting as their agents will apply for the incentives. Therefore, for all practical purposes the program reaches the same client groups that purchased flow-through shares before, and it brings approximately the same benefits which the earned depletion deduction would have provided to June, 1988.
While CEIP is aimed at junior companies that issue flowthrough shares for exploration activities, it is nevertheless acceptable by both public and private companies. However, CEIP is designed to encourage new investment capital for exploration. The regulations must include special rules to ensure that only exploration activity rather than developmental financed by this equity will qualify. These rules will be covered in the regulations which will be developed after consultation with industry and the Department of Finance, hopefully sometime this summer or very early fall.
For most investors the program will provide greater benefits than earned depletion. Repayment will be just as fast because firms will be able to submit applications four times per year. They will be able to submit them through five new regional offices that will themselves make a contribution to regional economic development.
Since announcing CEIP on May 3, we have been in constant consultation with the industry. In fact, at the end of May, we sent out a discussion paper entitled Proposed Rules for Canadian Exploration Program to obtain the views of the relevant industry associations, provincial and territorial Governments, and key investment community planners. In general we have received in general very favourable responses to this paper.
Over the summer months while officials in my Department are drafting regulations for this Bill, we will address the technical questions arising from our consultative process. Consultation rather than confrontation is a very important policy of this Government and it will be continued. Reasoned discussions about problems will lead to equitable solutions within the spirit of this program.
June 28, 1988

In conclusion, this program provides financial incentives that do not run counter to the Government's tax reform initiatives. It maintains a balance between the oil, gas and mining sectors with respect to opportunities to raise funds for much needed exploration. It allows the industry to make decisions and allows the investors to make decisions. It is not a discretionary, bureaucratically driven grants program.

Historically, flow-through shares have enhanced prosperity in many isolated regions in Canada where there is often only one industry other than mining or oil and gas.
In particular, this program will ensure that these regions will continue to benefit from the profits earned through exploration financed by flow-through shares.

In my opinion, when economically disadvantaged regions of our country benefit from such a program as CEIP, then all of Canada benefits as well. The program we are establishing by passing this piece of legislation today is a good one and is supported by the mining industry, by the equity industry, and by the exploration industry. It fulfils a need and will ensure adequate exploration in Canada over the short term and mid term. This legislation deserves our full support.

Mr. Speaker, we in this Party have no option but to support this legislation because in fact the initiative began with this Party. A rose by any other name smells as sweet, and that is the situation we have here. This is not simply a name change but a change in the mechanism to a system of passing out cheques rather than a system of allowing people to withhold taxes. In any case, it amounts to the same thing.
To listen to the Minister, one would think that suddenly a light had gone on in the Government's head with regard to a great new regional development incentive. The fact is quite the opposite. As a matter of fact, the March 12 edition of Daily Press, northeastern Ontario's daily newspaper, contains the following headlines: "Liberal critic watches Wilson", "Finance Minister dismantling tool", and in a separate item, "NDP finance critic changes his tune on funding scheme".
The reality is that this measure was brought in by this Party when we were in government in 1983, a measure which has been eminently successful. After 1983, it took off as the source of 70 per cent of the financing behind mining exploration. It was a successful regional development tool. It was an idea that worked. It brought in hundreds of millions of dollars of investment to small mining companies in remote regions of Canada, and it created thousands of jobs.
What happened to it? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) saw fit to discontinue it. Yesterday, in the debate on the Estimates, we heard of all the jobs that had been created in Canada by the present Government. Jobs may have been created, but where have they been created? They have been created mostly in Toronto, not in the regions.
Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act
This was an initiative that created jobs in the regions where jobs were needed. The Minister just said that in his speech, and that is quite true. However, the purpose of the Minister of Finance was to do away with that program which provided hundreds of millions of dollars to small mining companies and therefore to put into jeopardy the thousands of jobs that had been created and the new jobs that might be created.
This was not really a deathbed repentance on the part of the Government, either. It was only through a great deal of pressure from a very formidable lobby headed by people from Kirkland Lake and Timmins in northern Ontario, and from Val d'Or and other mining areas in Quebec, a coalition of concerned mayors, company executives and individuals from all of those regions, that the Government was forced to change its mind.
As a matter of fact, this is really a rerun of the drama of pension deindexing. The very same thing happened. The Government decided to stop the indexing of old age pensions and there was a hue and cry across the country. Grey power rose up in the thousands all across Canada, and there was enough pressure in support of the Opposition's attacks upon the Government that the policy was changed. The same thing happened on flow-through shares.
The Minister of Finance decided that creating jobs in Toronto was enough, and he decided to do away with flowthrough shares. This powerful lobby came together and supported the Opposition in its attack on the Government. As a result, the Government's policy was changed. That is the reality.
We met with this coalition, the Canadian Save Flow Through Committee, on March 1. The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) and I met with that group. It explained to us its great concern that the regions would be affected and that small mining companies which had work in progress would not be able to bring that exploration to fruition.
The Minister is quite right. It is not just northern Ontario and northern Quebec that benefits from this measure. In my own province there is gold exploration and exploration for other minerals on the island of Newfoundland. That exploration is about to come on stream, and it was thrown into jeopardy by this move.
We met with that coalition on March 1, and our finance critic, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Gameau), emphasized in his speech to the group that the retention of this deduction would constitute an important facet of the regional development strategy of future Liberal Governments. It was this Party that brought in the initiative in 1983. It will be this Party that continues to have that initiative in our program as a successful tool for regional development.
The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides also noted that flow-through shares represented a practical instance of co-

June 28, 1988
Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act
operation between the private sector and the Government since, as the Minister said in his speech as well, and on that point he was quite right, they avoided the bureaucratic red tape which often comes with direct subsidies. That is the reality, and we in the Liberal Party not only want to continue this initiative but to see it created as a box of tax incentives which perhaps would function in a manner similar to RSPs.
This is not something that the Government has suddenly discovered. It is not a light that has gone on in the Government's head. Rather, it is a baseball bat that was beaten over the Government's head to bring it to its senses with regard to a sensible regional development policy. It is an idea that worked. It is an idea that the Government wanted to stop. It is an idea that, thank God, is going to be continued because of the pressure from this Party.
I would like also to quote from the March 12 edition of the Daily Press which carried the following headline:
NDP finance critic changes his tune on funding scheme.
The article went on to say:
Michael Cassidy is not one to make apologies.
The personable New Democratic finance critic in the House of Commons readily admits he was totally against the concept of flow-through shares as recently as December 1986.
I will read that again.
The personable New Democratic finance critic in the House of Commons readily admits he was totally against the concept of flow-through shares as recently as December 1986.
The article continued:
At that time, he said he felt flow-throughs benefited only Bay Street and large investors.
Who does he represent? Not the place I come from. However, he has changed his mind and thank God for that. The article went on to quote him as saying:
"I have given a lot of thought to flow-throughs and the depletion allowance in the last year or so,"-
If it takes a year, then let it take a year as long as they come up with good policies. He said:
"But they have turned into quite a regional development tool."
That is true. We knew that in 1983. That is why the then Liberal Minister of Finance brought in this legislation. It has worked, so we support it. We have no option because it is creating jobs in eastern Canada, northern Ontario, northern Quebec, and northern B.C., as well as, obviously, in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Those areas need job creation.
This is not a hand-out. This is an investment that is paying off in jobs. It is one that this Party, the originator of the idea, fully supports now and well into the future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point to the minority report that we submitted at the time the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs issued its report on tax reform. You will recall that the committee itself had a number of questions about the flow-through mechanism and recommended changes in what the Government was doing. Recommendation No. 9 of the NDP minority report urged the development of tax measures specifically targeted to smaller companies and to regions in need of investment. We stated in the fall of last year that the flow-through share provisions had benefited small companies but were so broadly designed that large, well-established corporations which did not need the assistance had also benefited.
When my friend from Labrador speaks to this issue he suggests that the Liberal program of 1983 was sufficiently desirable that it should have been maintained in its entirety. However, it was the abuses that arose under that program which eventually led to the need to take some action. When companies like Falconbridge, Inco, and Cominco took advantage of the flow-through provisions meant to benefit junior mining companies and promote new investment and new mines, it was clear that something was wrong. However, just as the Liberals had thrown away billions of taxpayers' dollars on the scientific research tax credit, there was also the threat that that would occur with the flow-through provision as designed by the Liberals and perpetuated for a while by the Progressive Conservatives.
The Hon. Member is correct that in the fall of 1986 my Party questioned the whole flow-through mechanism as it existed because of the abuses which had been put in place by the Liberals and perpetuated by the Progressive Conservatives. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) then turned around and decided to throw out the baby with bath water by throwing out the whole mechanism in a very brief phase-out. That created enormous inequity since there was a continuing program for the oil and gas industry similar to what is being enacted today which was not provided for the mining industry. It created enormous concerns in areas of northern Quebec, northern

Ontario, and the West which had simply not benefited. They had not had a chance to benefit from any regional development programs from the Liberals or Progressive Conservatives. Yet this was a program, as they pointed out so effectively, that was working. I will cite the estimates made by prospectors in Quebec, for example.

A study done by the Association des prospecteurs du Quebec, for example, found that the flow-through share mechanism, an incentive associated with the mining sector, had contributed to 71 share issues in 1985, of which 33 involved flow-through shares, and to 25 strikes. It is estimated that these strikes will generate profits and jobs in the future. Mr. Speaker, the residents and the communities that would like the flow-through share program to continue have shown how effective this program has been in depressed areas where the rate of unemployment was running as high as 20 per cent, as was the case in the riding of the Honourable Member for Abitibi (Mr. St-Julien).

Six per cent, according to the Member for Abitibi, all as a result of this program, Mr. Speaker. And what did the Conservative government do after dismantling the program in terms of providing specific benefits to regions such as the Abitibi and northern Manicouagan? It abandoned these regions. And it abandoned the Members representing these regions, Mr. Speaker. A campaign was launched by the New Democratic Party, by the Liberal Party, by prospectors, by the junior mining companies, by the chambers of commerce .. . For instance, a coalition was formed in Quebec. It included universities, CEGEP's, unions, chambers of commerce, mining associations, junior mining companies and so forth. Everyone was involved, even the Quebec government. The municipalities also jumped into the fray.
In the end reason prevailed. When I say that reason prevailed, I refer to the recommendations which we made about eight or nine months ago to urge the development of tax measures specifically targeted to smaller companies and regions in need of investment. Through Bill C-137, the Government has come up with a program which provides for a substitute for the earned depletion allowance in the form of the 30 per cent incentive payment on qualified exploration
Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act
expense. The term "Qualified corporation" has been defined and this will require some study. I hope this Bill has a chance to go to committee briefly because I would like to ensure that the words are okay. However, "qualified corporation" has been defined, as I understand it, in such a way as to ensure that major mining companies will not be able to draw tens of millions of dollars from this program as they were able to do from the flow-through share mechanism which existed previously under the Liberals and Conservatives. The Hon. Minister says that they will probably not bother because the maximum incentive in a year will be about $3 million.
They have not eliminated but have certainly limited the use of the flow-through mechanism for step out exploration by companies like Falconbridge and Inco, which I believe was a major abuse. At the time mineral prices were low, Falcon-bridge stepped in and took advantage of this program for its routine annual program of exploration, designed to ensure that 10 or 12 years of reserves are always available as a part of the normal functioning of its mine in Sudbury. I felt that was an abuse.
There is, therefore, a limitation of $10 million and a cap on maximum expenditure, although I am not quite clear what happens if the applications for funding exceed the cap. The Minister may want to comment on that at a later date. This means that the Government has now accepted the type of advice it was receiving from the industry and communities affected which saw that so much of this activity was coming from junior mining companies that would not have been able to carry out the exploration expenditure without the incentive of the flow-through program and the mineral exploration depletion allowance which are now being replaced with the incentives in this particular program.
In other words, we now have a program specifically targeted to smaller companies. It is not regionally located, but most mining activity does not take place on the outskirts of Toronto. It takes place in northern Quebec. It takes place in Labrador. It takes place in northern Ontario, it takes place in the northern parts of the Prairies and Territories, and in the interior and north of British Columbia, areas which otherwise would be suffering from high levels of unemployment, areas which have been ignored by government far too long, and in many cases areas where there are single-industry towns whose only hope under existing Governments of continuing to thrive and prosper is the discovery of new mineral deposits and the development of them within reach of their workforce, in order that people can move from one mine to another as old mines become less productive and profitable.
I make no apologies for the fact that the New Democratic Party, and myself as spokesperson, questioned the generosity, the scope, and the lack of focus of the flow-through mechanism in 1986; nor do I make any apology for the fact that we as a Party which has a skeptical view of corporate tax incentives listened to the people, the communities, and the industry concerned with respect to whether or not there was a means by which the flow-through mechanism could be enhanced,

It is one thing to be skeptical and another thing, as I said, simply to say "no" categorically under any circumstances. My leader has made it clear that where it appears that an incentive to business is working effectively in terms of promoting jobs, research, economic development, and equality for women and minorities, to which I believe every Member of this House in all Parties would subscribe, and where it is clear that the benefits equal or exceed the cost of that particular incentive, that particular program should be considered very seriously.
That does not mean that it should be automatically accepted. There may be other means of better using the public's dollars. We must always remember that a dollar put into an incentive for junior mining corporations, for example, is a dollar which cannot be spent on other programs such as a national child care program, an affirmative action program for women or, dare I say it, a contribution to peace and common security by means of an improvement in our foreign aid program.
We must be careful with these dollars. However, we have said very consistently that where it is demonstrated that there is a real benefit, it makes sense to consider the matter very seriously. It is in that spirit that the New Democratic Party supports the principle embedded in Bill C-137 which is before us today.
I believe that the Government and the Liberal Party are to be criticized for the fact that the Government turned topsyturvy on this and for the fact that both the Government and the Official Opposition from time to time have been totally blind to the wasteful use and misuse of incentives to the corporate sector. The Liberals brought in the scientific
research tax credit about 1981 or 1982 and it was a bonanza. The stock markets and promoters in Vancouver, Montreal, and particularly Toronto, rubbed their hands with glee. In short order they had put together programs which have successfully taken $700 million or $800 million out of the pockets of average Canadians and put it into the hands of promoters for research, much of which has proven to be useless, not well founded and, in many cases, not well intended, and which under any circumstances have been an arrogant and total waste of public funds.
The Liberals drew on a very strong tradition which began with the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) when he was Minister of Finance in the early 1970s. He began this tradition of give aways to the corporate sector for which there was no ground at all. That has been carried on by the Progressive Conservatives. In fact, they let another $1 billion or more go out the door through the scientific research tax credit before they finally stopped up that tax loophole. It was as if they had cut an artery and let the taxpayers' money flow into the pockets of people who are now sitting back and laughing at the stupidity of the Liberal and Conservative Parties.
Let me come back to the question of flow-through shares and the tax reform proposals. The Finance and Economic Affairs Committee did a useful job in its work on this particular subject in the last year and a half. In our study of the White Paper on tax reform during the summer and fall last year we closely considered this question and said that there had to be an alternative mechanism. We argued strongly that the Department of Finance timetable for phasing out the earned depletion allowance was unfair, far too short, and would create enormous difficulties in the mining sector. Of course, that has occurred.
I believe that has occurred not solely because of the stock market collapse in October last year but because there has been a general continuation of economic activities. Most sectors have not experienced a sharp cut-back because of the stock market crash.
However, this announcement has hung like the sword of Damocles over the Canadian mining industry, particularly the junior mines for some time. The large mining companies have not been affected because they returned to profitability a year or two ago. Their mineral prices have been high and rising rapidly. Their profits have been quite substantial, and they were able to write off their exploration and development expenditures from their profits. They did not need to take advantage of the earned depletion allowance and flow-through share system.
However, the smaller companies that were not in a tax paying position were badly affected. What has occurred since then could best be described as a pre-election strip-tease by the Government. In December, in response to the recommendations of the Finance Committee, the Government decided to
June 28, 1988

extend by six months the final phase out of the 16 and two-thirds per cent earned depletion allowance to the end of 1989. Originally it was due to expire at the beginning, then the middle of 1989.
It is my understanding that the Hon. Minister is announcing that the present rate of earned depletion allowance will be extended to the end of 1989. I believe that is a change from what was already intended. Finally, we have legislation which I have indicated my Party supports.
There should be a lesson from this. We had a program that was well intended, had proven to be effective in terms of helping the mining industry in remoter parts of Canada, but which had faults at the same time. Too much of the benefit was going to either very wealthy investors or large mining companies, rather than junior mining companies developing new mines.
That program has been substituted with a program that will be substantially more modest in its cost. It is estimated to have an annual cost of about $70 million a year. The Minister's White Paper estimated that the cost of the flow-through mechanism might have been as high as $300 million a year. We have effected a substantial saving to the Treasury and have a program that is more targeted.
The third point is that the industry came to us, as it went to the Minister of State and the Government, to say that it does not want a program whereby it must make an application every time it believes it can do exploration. It does not want a program like the regional development incentive in which it must pass proposals by a bureaucrat in order to gain approval. It would like an assurance that its judgment would be trusted. Therefore it is prepared to spend $7 or $8 on an exploration program on which it can get back some money. For every $10 of qualified expenditure there will be a 30 per cent incentive or rebate. That means the industry will spend $7 and the Government will be prepared to chip in $3 in incentives.
The industry also said that it would prefer such a program. The New Democratic Party listened to that proposal carefully and looked at some of the alternatives. It is proving possible to focus the program in such a way that that particular wish of the mining industry is being satisfied. The industry will make the decisions about where explorations should go and what kind of exploration should proceed. If a mining company finds a promising new prospect and does not want to tip off its competitors about it, it can proceed with its drilling and stake its claim prior to notifying a government official about what it is doing, and still qualify for the exploration incentive. I believe that reflects how the program is being designed to be sensitive to the needs of the original industry.
There were legitimate questions about the cost of the program and its focus. It seemed that too much money was going to large companies that did not need the incentives and that the program should have focused on smaller companies. If it is possible to take that program and improve it, it should be possible in other areas as well.
Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act
My party believes that an exploration incentive program would ensure the health of the mining industry, and in particular the health of the smaller companies. This program is an example of what other incentives could do for manufacturing industries. For instance, instead of handing out all kinds of incentives to people in the hope that jobs will be created, specific areas could be targeted to ensure that the taxpayers' money is not being wasted and that the benefits arising from the federal program are in line with the costs to the taxpayer.
I believe that in future, when we have, I hope, the opportunity to design a fairer, more equitable tax system than the old one, even though it was instituted by the Conservative Party's white paper and tax reform proposal, it will be possible in many sectors to effect the same kind of reform as that proposed today in Bill C-137.
I would like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying to my friend from Abitibi (Mr. St-Julien), who worked for this with the Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) ... it should be remembered that those Members had to seek support in industry and the Opposition parties.
Our party, as the Honourable Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) noted in his quotation from the North Bay Nugget, I believe, or the Timmins Press, affirmed its support for the flow-through shares program in March 1987, only two or three months after objecting to the previous program as a whole. However, it took the Minister of State (Forestry and Mines) (Mr. Merrithew) and the Minister of finance (Mr. Wilson) until May 1988 to issue a joint statement to the effect that, finally, the government would do something to meet the needs of regions affected by the government's decision to eliminate flow-through shares and previous incentives.
Mr. Speaker, it has taken 14 months, and it is only through the efforts of the people of the minig regions, such as my friend the former rector of the University of Quebec at Abitibi, Mr. Rene Trudel, that this issue has come before the House of Commons. It is through the efforts of the Association des prospecteurs du Quebec and other associations, of all the flowthrough share committees, the people who came here with their "Go with the flow" buttons to support flow-through shares. It is primarily through their efforts, Mr. Speaker, that the government was finally persuaded.
If the Member for Abitibi and his colleague from Timiskaming, Ontario, had had to go it alone, there would have been no change and mining areas would be in very difficult economic straits because of the decline in exploration that is ending already and will become worse in the coming months.
It is because our party was prepared to look at the region's needs objectively, to work with people there, to indicate, as we have done today, that we are ready, despite the Free Trade Agreement, despite everything else we are opposed to, to co-

June 28, 1988
Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act
operate in ensuring that this bill is passed. Mr. Speaker, it is thanks to all that, ultimately, that this step forward has been taken.
As I just said, I believe the details must be given some consideration. I don't know how this could be worked out, perhaps a legislative committee could spend two or three days on it. I don't know what discussions have been held among the House Leaders of the three parties regarding referral of this Bill to Committee. I have some questions about that, simply to reassure myself that, for example, this is really a program for junior mining companies and not a disguised program with hidden benefits for the big mining companies that won't be getting benefits. But although I'm suggesting referral to a legislative committee, I know we are committed to ensuring passage of the Bill before we adjourn in July for the summer recess, for the holidays, and we will keep that promise.
Thank you for your patience and attention, Mr. Speaker. I think it's an historic occasion to see the support we are showing for a Conservative Party bill, and to see how generously the Conservatives applauded our Party's support for their motion.

My questions really relate to the two points I raised in my speech. Perhaps I can raise them with the Minister who is here now. To what extent is the definition of eligible expenses reduced? To what extent is it still possible for these large enterprises in Vancouver and Toronto to continue to package flow-through investments under this particular program? Is that a healthy kind of situation or not? To what extent, if at all, can large companies benefit under this particular program?
There is a $70 million cap on expenditures. What is the intention of the Government if it finds that the rate in which this fund is drawn down is going more quickly than had been anticipated? Is it the Government's intention to judge that the program is a success and reduce the percentage rate of incentive from 30 per cent to a lower figure? Or, is it the Government's intention that this in fact is an open-ended commitment?
Those are the major questions I had hoped might be answered. I might come back to one or two of them, but if the Hon. Minister has some comment on those questions now it would be helpful.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just on the first point, the Act spells out very, very carefully under Section 5 that the eligible expenses which can be used by a qualified company using a flow-through share mechanism are exactly the same as they were before and as defined under the Income Tax Act. There are no changes whatsoever. It worked before. It is exactly the same mechanism.
Second, the Member asked what the role would be, whether CMP and some of those very large equity raising companies would be operating about the same. Yes, they will. In fact, they have already gone to the equity market-place with some packages. Limited partnerships will be put together as in the past. There is no change there.
Third, the Member asked to what extent large companies would be able to utilize this particular program. I can tell him that I have talked with quite a lot of seniors in the Mining Association of Canada. It is very unlikely that they would use it at all. It makes no sense for them. First of all, they may not have losses which they can write off, and they are unlikely to want to deplete their own share ownership and give it to investors through a limited partnership. They would much rather hang on to their shares and invest out of their cash flow.
I have an idea that they would be very unlikely to undertake that. I guess the good side of it is that the larger companies will tend to have their own exploration programs as they mostly had in the past.
June 28, 1988

This program, because of the cap, is designated for junior mining companies. I believe those are the three or four issues the Member raised.

Should the draw downs of money go above the $70 million at the current rate of 30 per cent, is it the Government's intention, should it still be the Government, as a matter of policy that the incentive rates would be adjusted to keep the annual draw down at about $70 million? Member that the amount that was to be drawn down from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, which is mentioned in this particular Bill, will cover the draw on it through the hydrocarbon part which is a replacement for CEDIP effective October 1 and through to the end of this fiscal year, March 31, 1989. Although no one will know, we think that there will be a adequate number of dollars in there to finance both programs. If not, we can always undertake to raise money the way we normally do if one program happens to be running short of cash.
I can tell the Hon. Member that the 30 per cent of the contribution on the incentive toward eligible expenses will be in place for two full years. At the end of that time we will have a look at it to see if the level of exploration is satisfactory. If it is, we will continue. Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the first question had to do with the relative levels of expenditures that would be required to fund this particular initiative. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: Could the Minister say what is the status of these subsidies under the trade agreement? subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just to make sure that we understand the figures in the previous question, it is around $150 million for the mineral exploration side and about $60 million for the oil and gas or hydrocarbons. It is for a total of about $210 million for a full fiscal year. That is with the proviso that we do not know what it will really cost, because we do not know the level of activity. We think it will be adequate.
With respect to the Hon. Member's question on whether or not I think there is any conflict with the free trade agreement which is being worked out now, no, we do not think that there is at all. As the Hon. Member probably knows, this initiative is directed toward juniors, or very basic grass roots exploration. It is not a subsidy given to, for example, gold, zinc, antimony, or potash. It is available for just general grass roots exploration. From every source which we have checked we anticipate that there will be no conflict at all.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I want to commend the Minister on this legislation, Bill C-137. I am sure that the

June 28, 1988
Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act
program will assist small and medium sized explorers to raise capital. However, I have two concerns. The first has to do with arm's length and the other has to do with eligible expenses.
In his remarks the Minister mentioned that the regulations would be forthcoming at perhaps the end of the summer or early fall after consulting with the industry. I wonder if the Minister would give favourable consideration to the removal of the words "where the corporation and investor are at arm's length from the eligible expenses". There are numerous privately owned oil and gas exploration companies in the industry. I believe that this consideration would provide privately owned oil and gas exploration companies the same opportunities as provided for public companies under the present terms of the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program. Some small private companies will find it very difficult to issue more shares. It will really cause dilution of the company.
I want the Minister to comment on what expenditures qualify. Using the Income Tax Act, which the Minister mentioned in his remarks, really discriminates against the petroleum industry. The problem with the Income Tax Act is the threat of a potential retroactive assessment by the tax Department. That is sort of reclassifying a well from exploration to development.
This happens when a well appears to strike a new oil or a gas pool and then later when the geology is better understood it is decided that it hit upon an existing pool. A reassessment is then made under the provisions of the Income Tax Act. The entitlement that is paid through the CEIP, which has probably gone out to the investors, is really null and void and would have to be collected back. Would the Minister talk about arm's length also in regard to what expenditures qualify?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Calgary South. She has been very assiduous in trying to protect the interests of those small privately owned exploration companies on the oil and gas side.
I want to say what we have tried to do. The industry asked us in our consultations to use the same type of criterion under eligible expenses that would be given under Section 66 of the Income Tax Act. The industry said: "Leave it as it is. It is working now". We are happy with that so we will leave it that way. There will be no retroactive assessments. We are attempting to ensure that that does not happen.
The other one is a much more difficult one to resolve. That is the issue of small exploration companies on the oil and gas side. We have to remember that CEIP is not like CEDIP which is essentially an activity program. A tax mechanism is being used here. When the program was designed we wanted to ensure that it utilized the flow-through share mechanism. It was very important that we maintain that as a means to flow through those benefits to individual shareholders. If that is not done, there is some concern that there could be a potential for abuse. For example, one corporation could flow shares to
another shareholder, perhaps other small shareholders within the same corporation, or a wholly owned subsidiary. There is more potential for abuse using the other route and not having it at arm's length.
I wish it to be fully understood that CEIP is utilizing a tax mechanism. The idea is to find a way to raise equity for exploration. We do not want this to move in and find another way of doing it, if we do not have to use the tax system form. The rules do not preclude a private company making a private placement to existing shareholders, providing that shareholder is not the majority shareholder in that corporation or a member of a related group in which he would be a majority shareholder. In other words, while it might preclude the majority, it does not preclude any small company from utilizing the mechanism, providing it is not to the majority shareholder who already has control of that company.
There is one thing I will make in accommodation to the Hon. Member for Calgary South. We have had many consultations with the industry, not only the exploration industry on the oil and gas side but on the mineral side and through the investment community.
We will undertake to continue that type of discussion with them. We understand their concerns. We too have concerns about it. Perhaps something might be able to be worked out. I am not sure. We will undertake, on behalf of the Hon. Member for Calgary South and on behalf of other Members who share those views, to consider the interests of those small privately owned exploration companies on the energy side. We will undertake to work out the regulations with them. Hopefully we can come to a meeting of minds. We wish to be very careful that we do not, in some way, leave ourselves open to potential abuse by manipulating the shares between one company or a corporation and its wholly owned subsidiaries. We have to be careful of that, and we will do the best. I appreciate the Hon. Member's views in this matter.

The previous program was called CEDIP. With the type of turnaround that the Government has done, the new program might very well be called "CEDIP-CEDOO-DLE".
In the unfortunate event that the Party of the Hon. Member is likely to form the Government after the next election-

-what type of dipsy-doodling will be done in 1990 when the review is done? What will be the factors in the review? Will it take another stock market crash before we see a continuation of flow through? Can we assure the industry now, particularly the Prospectors and Developers Association?
June 28, 1988

I think it should be put on record, the contribution of the Prospectors and Developers Association and of the flowthrough share committee with its chairperson, Eveline Kasner.
I would particularly mention the mayors of Kirkland Lake and Val d'Or who did an excellent job in the lobby process.
The question really becomes: Will we have to go through the lobby process in 1990? Will it take a stock market crash in 1990, or on what factors will the review process be done? What weight will be given to those various factors?
Mir. Merrithew: Like the Lion. Member, I have no crystal ball to see what the conditions might be like in the equity markets generally in Canada at the end of 1990. One thing we can assure the Hon. Member is that we will consult, as we have now, with groups such as the prospectors and developers, APQ in Quebec, the Mining Association of Canada and, of course, the CMPs, and the NIMs. on the investment side. We have already consulted widely with them. We will continue to do so.
Essentially, the reason we might have to change the level of contribution either up or down would be the level of mining exploration activity that we might have going on. We were forced to take this particular step. It was something totally out of the hands of anyone. That is what happened on October 19 in the stock market. Obviously we saw what was probably going to be a very adequate level of exploration expenditure suddenly disappear. This group will need help. We immediately started to consult with them and ask: "How can we do this?" We extended MEDA to the end of 1988 and brought in this program. Those two things would determine what we would have to do with the 30 per cent. There are two full years in which to deal with the level of expenditures, the grass roots expenditures, and the need for raising of equity by those small companies that do not have many other mechanisms by which they can raise equity for exploration.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I ask the Hon. Minister what would be the interplay of the earned depletion allowance continuing in 1989 at the lower rate and of the new incentive programs coming in for mining at the same time. Will the regulations be designed in such a way that it is not possible to stack one on top of the other, but that the total benefit will be in the order of the 30 per cent incentive? How will the Minister handle that particular problem?
As a final comment, because I believe it is time that we started going through the sections fairly quickly, as a finance critic I am uneasy that a complex piece of legislation similar to tax legislation should be adopted by the House within a matter of a day or less from it being introduced in the House. I believe that the delays were due to the Government. It has taken from May 3 to June 26 or June 27 for the Bill to be introduced. That is inadequate. I hope the Senate has a more profound look at it and will abide by the agreement that we gave to see this through. It is not good to legislate in this particular manner. I sincerely hope there are no egregious errors in the Bill as a consequence of its hasty passage. It is a bad way to
Canadian Exploration Incentive Program Act
proceed. I hope that the Department of the Hon. Minister and the Department of Finance together ensure that this type of hasty treatment is not given to such future complex and important legislation. After all, we are engaging in the expenditure of $200 million a year. In anybody's language that is a lot of money.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not share the view of the Hon. Member that there has been any inappropriate hastiness in this particular program. It is a complicated program because it does utilize other references to different pieces of legislation, for example the Income Tax Act and CEDIP. It was not an easy piece of legislation to put together. We wanted to take our time at it, and we did, in order to consult with the industry, and it appreciated that. We will continue that type of process. Most of the detail will come out in the regulations under the Act, not this piece of legislation which by itself is reasonably general.
On the Mining Exploration Depletion Allowance, under CEDIP on the energy side, that will continue at 16 and two-thirds per cent. Applicants who wish to utilize this particular mechanism will have a choice of going with one or the other. They can use either or an accommodation, but they cannot exceed the level outlined in the Act which is 30 per cent of a maximum of $10 million of eligible exploration expenditures.
On the mining side MEDA will continue at 33 and one-third per cent until the end of 1988 and will then be phased out to zero. They will go immediately into the new program which is as rich or even a bit richer.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The point that I make on the process is that if it is a complicated piece of legislation as the Minister states, and if it required a great deal of preparation, what is the basis of the assumption by his officials that Parliament can then turn around and pass it in the blink of an eye? If there were consultations widely within the industry, there could have also been consultations within the House of Commons. If the industry were only consulted narrowly, then there will be many companies that may have wanted to make some comments but would have been excluded from the consultation process.
Therefore, I suggest as a general rule that it is not good to legislate in this manner. I am afraid that all of us are familiar with the problems that arise when legislation is rushed through the House too hastily. I am saying this at the same time as recognizing that my Party has called for this type of legislation and is happy to see it go through. In process terms we run severe risks because of the way this is being handled.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO WORK OF SERVICE PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Saturday, June 25, was Armed Forces Day in Canada.
The members of our Armed Forces are called upon to perform many tasks and, as a result, they have developed an expertise and professionalism in a very extensive variety of duties and responsibilities. Whether they are called upon to handle natural disasters caused by floods, fire, or earthquakes, they assume those duties with poise, efficiency and good naturedness.
Because of their ability to be good soldiers, and diplomats in their understanding of international politics, they have performed peacekeeping duties whenever called upon to do so. Their emphasis on training and their ability to meet new challenges make them an efficient and respected security force in the international community.
All Canadians I am sure will recognize that the members of the Canadian Armed Forces do Canada proud as they perform their duties of national and international security, with diplomacy and tact, anywhere in the world.
This Parliament of Canada thanks them for their dedication and efforts.

Mr. Speaker, in 1905 a great Prime Minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, refused to entrench French in the Alberta Charter as the vast majority of the population in the new province were English-speaking Canadians
In 1988 a great Premier, Hon. Don Getty, and his Attorney General, Hon. Jim Horsman, and their PC supporters made English the language of legislation in Alberta because 97 per cent of the population are English-speaking Canadians. After all, a real democratic Government reflects the thinking of the majority of its electors in its laws, and both Laurier and Getty have done this. Furthermore, Premier Getty is operating within the Constitution, and Alberta's treatment of its minorities, including the French minority, is equal or better than that found in any other province.
I support the position taken by the Alberta Government as it is in direct accordance with the thinking of the people of the province to whom the Government is accountable, and that is democracy, Mr. Speaker.
