LA CENTRALE DE L'ENSEIGNEMENT DU QUEBEC
LA CENTRALE DE L'ENSEIGNEMENT DU QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Centrale de Venseignement du Quebec set a precedent yesterday by electing a woman, Lorraine Page, president. Ms. Page becomes the first woman in Quebec to lead a large labour union. The openness of the union movement to women is remarkable. We see Ms. Page's accession to the highest position in the Centrale de l'enseignement du Quebec as a result of the evolution in thinking that, we hope, will occur in all segments of our society.
The CEQ did not elect a token woman but a real president who sees her election this way, "I am rather inclined to believe that the fruit falls when it is ripe."
Ms. Page has proved her ability and leadership as president of the Montreal Teachers' Alliance. We wish her every possible success in her new duties, because we know that she will devote all her enthusiasm, determination and energy to them. I am sure that Ms. Page as president of the CEQ will represent the workers well, as does Shirley Carr, president of the Canadian Labour Congress.



June 28, 1988

Mr. Speaker, today the Serbian community in Canada celebrates Serbian Day, a day on which Serbian Canadians celebrate their rich culture, heritage, and tradition, and commemorate an important event in Serbian history, the Battle of Kosovo.
Serbian immigration to Canada began in the second half of the 19th century. Many of those who followed came in search of the freedom denied them in their homeland. Over the years, Canadians of Serbian descent have made significant contributions to the cultural, social and economic development of Canada and have taken great pride in their dual heritage. They have retained, enhanced and shared their heritage, and today the Serbian community in Canada invites all Canadians to join them in celebrating Serbian Day.

Mr. Speaker, Firestone has done it again. It ought to get the worst citizen of the year award in the country of Canada.
Having collected upon a $13.5 million interest free grant for five years, and after picking up stakes, it has gone to the United States and left the Canadian workforce high and dry. To add insult to injury, this week we discovered that at the Hamilton area warehouse where it should be hiring laid-off Firestone workers, some of whom have more than 30 years' service, Firestone has decided to hire scabs to work in the warehouse.
Why doesn't the Government collect over $6 million in interest that it gave to this company so that it could rip off Canadian taxpayers, rip off the workers and go to the United States with machinery that was actually paid for by the people of Canada? Why doesn't the Government demand an immediate repayment of the $6 million in interest so that the workers in that company could at least get a fair shake by setting aside that particular money for a pension, retirement, and replacement fund?
Start fighting for the workers of this country, not fighting for American based multinationals that pick up stakes when the going gets tough.

Mr. Speaker, in this period of glasnost there are still hundreds of Jewish families who are suffering inhumane treatment at the hands of the Soviet authorities, and for what reason?
I speak particularly of Boris Bendersky and his family who were brought to my attention by one of my constituents. Mr. Bendersky is seriously ill with a kidney ailment that can only be treated by doctors in the West. However, the Soviet authorities refuse to let this family leave.
We must insist that the Soviet Union honour its signature on the Helskini Accords, that it act in a humane way and let these people have their freedom.

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
OPPOSITION TO ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite his best efforts the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) has failed miserably in his attempt to convince the Canadian people that this country needs a fleet of nuclear powered attack submarines.
In fact, it seems he is having a great deal of difficulty convincing even his own caucus colleagues of the need to spend billions and billions of dollars on these submerged nuclear power stations. Many of his colleagues are wisely urging him and the Government to abandon this dangerous proposal. Tory Members of Parliament are belatedly realizing what we on this side of the House have known for some time now, that Canadians don't want these submarines at any cost.
A recent slew of public opinion polls certainly must be discouraging to the Minister. One poll, done only last month, found that opposition to his megadollar proposal had soared to 60 per cent nationally. It is clear that Canadians have passed judgment on the Minister and his proposal. They see no need for Canada to get involved in the nuclear sub game. It is time the Government listened to this wise counsel.

ETOBICOKE ROTARY CLUB-ADMISSION OF WOMAN TO MEMBERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian women have been second-class citizens in law and still in many ways are second-class citizens in fact.

June 28, 1988
While Governments, including successive Governments here, have taken steps to see on the long journey to equality that this is changing, often progress comes when individuals and private organizations and individuals, men and women, join in this battle for true equality in Canadian society.
Today on the floor of the House I would like to pay tribute to the Etobicoke Rotary Club as being the first in Ontario to admit a woman to its membership and to point out that it intends to withstand the efforts being made by the head office of Rotary International in the United States to correct this development which they refer to as "a mistake", and to say through private organizations, like the Etobicoke Rotary Club, that we are seeing the spirit of equality of the sexes being achieved.
Not only do I pay tribute to this Rotary Club, I would also like to point out that I am very proud of the fact that the first woman to be admitted is the publisher of Etobicoke Life newspaper and my cousin, Lynne Boyer Parks.

Mr. Speaker, last Sunday, I had the opportunity to take part in a peaceful demonstration of officials from the south shore of Montreal. There were representatives from nearly 250 municipalities, several Members of this House and several Members of the National Assembly. And they were all together to denounce a situation that has gone on much too long, holding the people of the region hostage on the transportation issue.
Mr. Speaker, Highway 30 was promised several years ago and the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) when he was Minister of Transport made a commitment that a bridge would be built in the Salaberry-Valleyfield region, but this has not been done. Another transportation issue on the south shore of Montreal is the commitment made by the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) concerning the tolls on Champlain Bridge.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the people of the south shore are getting impatient, and rightly so, because of two commitments that this Government has not kept and unfortunately, last Sunday, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard), unlike his provincial counterpart, did not have the courage to come and explain his position to the people of this region.
Mr. Speaker, the voters on the south shore will not let themselves be bought at the last minute by another series of
promises from the Conservative Members. There must be a signed agreement and they must act immediately.

Mr. Speaker, deregulation has led to a continuing deterioration of airline services throughout northern Ontario. Since deregulation, jet service has been discontinued to Dryden and drastically reduced to Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury. Air Ontario has pulled out of Geraldton and Canadian Airlines has abandoned Dryden. Schedules have deteriorated, connection delays have increased, and transfers and overbooking have become more common.
In the meantime the major alternative, the Trans-Canada Highway, suffers from increasing truck traffic, is neglected by the provincial Government, and is totally ignored by the federal Government which provides funds for the Trans-Canada Highway in every other participating province.
I call upon the Government to abandon its slavish addiction to the ideologies of privatization and deregulation, to look at what is happening in real life to travellers in northern Ontario, and to establish a commission to examine the effect of deregulation on northern Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, the two-price wheat system has been abolished and grain farmers will receive compensation in the 1988-89 crop year to ease the process of adjustment. However, the real issue has become why the two-price wheat system was changed.
I have been disturbed by the recent comments of some western Canadians that the reason for the change was the free trade agreement. This hollow argument ignores the fact that the policy was no longer doing what it was intended to do. The two-price system was artificially distorting the production patterns for wheat in Canada while also taxing food.
Why should the Government continue to tax consumers and encourage the growing of grain outside the Wheat Board region when 17,000 Saskatchewan farmers and farm workers have left the land in the last year? Clearly the policy had to be changed because it was not helping the majority of grain farmers while it was hurting other sectors of the Canadian economy.
This Government has made a sustained commitment to agriculture that is based on sound judgment. The reality is that since this policy was no longer sound, it was ended for all Canadians.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to speak on Bill C-130. We believe this to be the most important economic agreement which Canada has ever signed. It is regrettable that we have this Bill before the House when we have not seen the United States legislation which would enable this agreement to become law. It is those types of concerns that cause great distrust among the Canadian people, not only of Government but of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and this whole agreement.
They are equally concerned because only five years ago when the Prime Minister was seeking the leadership of his Party he said in very determined and candid words that he was opposed to free trade with the United States. In fact, he said: "Canada rejected free trade with the United States in 1911. They will do it again in 1983".
My Party is not opposed to the liberalization of trade. We are opposed to the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal. We do not think that the Government got a very good deal out of it. It is not a free trade deal as such. It is a trade deal in which we did not get a great deal, and we gave away a lot.
The arguments that the Government is making for spending $30 million trying to sell this deal across the country are that it will give great access to the United States market, it is going to give secure access to the United States market, that it will give tremendous economic advantage to Canada, and that there is no alternative. Things are in such a terrible state that, even though the President has already vetoed the omnibus trade Bill, we have to jump off the cliff at any risk and accept this deal.
If we look at the deal itself we see what we have given away. We have given away or essentially aligned ourselves with the economy of the United States to make all of North America
June 28, 1988

one economy in which Canadian economic, trade, and industrial programs will be harmonized with those of the United States. We are turning over our water resources and our energy resources on an equal share basis. We are jeopardizing our social and environmental programs. When we start to harmonize economic policies, many other policies have to be harmonized, including social, cultural, and other programs.
In foreign investment the minimum goes to $150 million. Foreign investment will be able to come in and take over most Canadian companies without regard to providing any benefits to the Canadian economy. Our regional development programs will be affected because most of them under American trade law would be judged subject to countervail duties or antidumping duties. We will leap into the same economic basket with the United States service industry and financial institutions. All in all, we will give up a great deal.
I would like to look at the deal from the view of agriculture and the claims that the Government makes with regard to access to the U.S. market. Before doing so, I would like to mention the drafting instructions provided by the U.S. congressional committees, the Senate and the House committees, that went to the administration. They are very instructive. They tell us that this trade deal is subject to all other United States laws. It is interesting that our Bill C-130 is subject to the trade deal. Therefore, there is an inequity there. Not only is Bill C-130 subject to the trade deal, but any conflicts there are with provincial legislation will be subject to the trade deal as well, whereas on the American side, although we have not seen that Bill yet, its law will be superior to the trade deal.
Turning to the agriculture sector, if at some stage it is negotiated that we will do away with provincial marketing boards for the dairy industry, then Section 6 of the agreement on the implementing legislation or regulation can be drawn to do away with it. Those drafting instructions have a profound impact on all of agriculture.
Under Article 706 the administrative action recommended is that we get rid of all barriers for poultry and eggs. In Section 1901 there is a provision where the United States industry can put in place a permanent monitoring arrangement with reports to both industry and Congress in order that countervail or dumping duty actions can easily be taken by the United States industry.
Under these drafting instructions there is a section relating to the potato industry. It authorizes the United States administration to negotiate limits on imports of potatoes. There is a great deal in those drafting instructions to the United States administration which will end up in the United States Bill and will have a profound influence on Canadian agriculture.
Let us look at the argument the Government makes that we will have profound and great new access to the U.S. market. In the broad range of commodities traded with the United States the most commonly quoted one is the pork and beef industries. They will have great new access. Let us examine that situation.
Canada-U.S. Free trade Agreement
With regard to beef, over a five-year period we will remove the 1 cent per pound tariff on beef going into the United States. Essentially we have free trade now. I do not understand how we will have massive new access to the U.S. market with only 1 cent being removed over five years. Likewise, there is a countervail duty against hogs of $5 per hog. That stays in place. How will there be great new access?
The most troubling aspect and one of great concern to all exporters, whether in relation to beef, hogs, or any commodity, is the appreciation that has taken place in the Canadian dollar against the United States dollar. There has been almost a 15 per cent appreciation in the Canadian dollar. That was forecast, but most people did not think it would happen as rapidly. Clearly the Economic Council and some other agencies predicted that our dollar would appreciate from 70 cents in relation to the United States dollar during the next five or six years to toward 94 cents or 95 cents. Already we have seen an appreciation of 10 cents on our dollar against the United States dollar, which is far larger than any tariff advantage that will result from this trade deal.
In the Canada-U.S. meat import law, American meat import law drafting instructions suggest that the U.S. will still be able to use its meat import law if it is to carry out the impact of a third country importing that is subject to their meat import law, whereas our law does not provide for it. In fruits and vegetables, I have heard the Minister say that we may have an opportunity in a couple of commodities such as mushrooms, but generally our opportunities in fruits and vegetables are relatively limited in the U.S. Our controlled commodities of dairy and poultry products are far higher priced and there is little opportunity there. In the grains sector there is a tremendous market building up in the Pacific northwest for Canola meal. The western grain transportation subsidy is being removed almost immediately, whereas the tariff in place will be phased out over 10 years. There may be some increased access to the U.S. market, but it is extremely limited.
Let us look at coming the other way for the Canadian agriculture industry. In poultry, eggs, and turkeys, the U.S. has scored a major increase in its imports into Canada. The removal of tariffs on highly processed foods will increase that dramatically, as well as when those tariffs are removed. The CEMA organization has pointed out that there is a major problem with regard to surplus eggs, and that that will mean a further deterioration in the quota available in that sector.
In the dairy sector, the Government has moved to put in place import control regulations, but I think that we will wait a long time before we actually see any quantitative limitation. The grocery products manufacturing industry has made it clear right across the board that we cannot have supply managed and controlled commodities such as poultry and eggs and the goods processed from them being sold in this country and have them compete with eggs, poultry, and dairy commodities produced in the United States. The SAGITS told the Minister that in a report, and it has been ignored. Most

June 28, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free trade Agreement
processing food companies in this country are American controlled. Clearly 21 out of the 26 companies are. The industry sent a very definite signal that unless the Government gets rid of supply management in this country, within a matter of six or seven years it will be moving to the U.S. The pressure from the free trade deal, and through the GATT negotiations will be to get rid of supply management, which I think will be a disaster for the dairy industry and the poultry industry.
In the grain sector, we see that our two-price wheat system is going by the boards. Instead of consumers paying for their wheat when they buy their bread or grocery products, the Government will be providing a subsidy in that regard. Many people in the industry believe that the Canadian Wheat Board will be severely weakened, that it will not have the power to have import end use certificates, that they will be handled by the Canadian Grain Commission that in the long haul the Canadian Wheat Board will lose its power, and that we will come under the control of the multinational grain companies, which will gain greater and greater control. It is interesting that when the Government lists subsidies in the free trade agreement it lists the Western Grain Transportation Act as a $700 million subsidy. That is an historic arrangement that has been with us almost since the turn of the century. It is given to western farmers to make up for the costs of transportation. Nowhere in this agreement is it mentioned what the corps of engineers spent on the Mississippi River system. In the GATT negotiations the American industry will be trying to get rid of the Western Grain Transportation Act, transportation assistance.
There is no provision in this agreement to list what is spent on the Mississippi River transportation system. Perhaps in no area do we see a greater impact than in the fruit and vegetable industry. That industry will be severely hampered. It will lose its seasonal tariff it will not be able to keep it. The snap back provision to the most favoured nation tariff is a cumbersome, crude device which will not work. It is designed to replace the tariff that existed. If the price of fruits or vegetables in Canada drop below 90 per cent of the five-year average, a device like that which takes five to seven days to be put in place is a total joke. Once the price breaks on fresh fruits and vegetables, is gone for the season. No industry, of course, has suffered more than the grape industry, the wine industry. Even though this deal does not come into effect until next January, that industry is going through tremendous strife already. I talked to a producer in the Niagara escarpment over the weekend who has some 800 acres. I believe he is the largest producer of grapes in Canada. He said that his vines will have to be cut and removed. To give up those special fruit, vegetables, grape growing areas, to say that we can sacrifice them and that they are not very important is not a criminal act, but I think it would be a terrible decision for a Government to take. We would become dependent in future on the wine and grapes produced in California.
If the Government were to do this-and it is its decision-it should have had those adjustment programs well in place and even had them listed in the agreement so that they could not be countervailed themselves. This trade deal was a signal to the GATT that they could lower the boom on the Canadian wine industry, and in fact they have.
Fortunately, at least in Ontario, the Ontario Government has brought in arrangements to reduce the tariffs over 12 years. That is what the B.C. wine industry pleaded with the Minister to do. That is what the Minister said she would do and understood she had to do. If they had the 10 to 12 years they could have survived, but if they lose half the differential in price in one year they will not survive.
Similarly, this agreement is a signal to the GATT to get rid of Article 11 which in the get rid of supply management in this country, within the next seven or eight years.
With the pressure coming from the Americans at the GATT, the Cairns Group the grocery products manufacturers and others, I think the whole supply management industry will ultimately be destroyed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on a bill that will implement the historic agreement we have signed with the United States. Mr. Speaker, I intend, and I am sure this will come as a surprise, to vote in favour of the Bill.
At the Toronto Summit, heads of Government from the United Kingdom, Japan, France, Italy and the Federal Republic of Germany, and of course Canada and the United
States, spoke out in favour of the free trade agreement. They felt that the agreement was a positive step, not only for Canada and the United States but for all our major trading partners.
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, the free trade agreement is often discussed from a single perspective, as though it affected North America exclusively. In fact, we are talking about an agreement negotiated under the provisions of Article 24 of GATT. Furthermore, practically all the issues discussed by Canada and the United States during the bilateral talks are on the agenda of the multilateral trade negotiations now going on in Geneva.
That is why the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was right to say in his speech to the Americas Club in New York, and I quote:
At the multilateral level, a trade agreement between the two biggest trading
partners on this planet has exceptional significance. In fact, the outcome of the
GATT negotiations depends very much on this agreement.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may name a few of the issues: putting a stop to the introduction of new protectionist measures; preparing new rules for international trade in agricultural products; reducing or eliminating tariff and non-tariff barriers in order to improve market access; and developing basic principles for so-called new issues such as trade in services, intellectual property and trade-related investment.
The vocabulary is impressive and the concepts are high-sounding but basically, Mr. Speaker, it all boils down to this: All exporting countries are now part of an integrated world economy. As a result, they have to adopt trade policies that take into consideration the interests of their trading partners. For all practical purposes, the national market we have known for centuries is a disappearing bread.
That is the international reality that our country must fit into, Mr. Speaker. That is the reality on which the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States is based. However-and this will surprise you too, Mr. Speaker-some among us refuse to see this reality.
Mr. Speaker, they are dealers in a big illusion. According to them, Canada can fully enjoy its interdependence with the world's main markets without at the same time exposing its companies and industries to international competition. They are greatly mistaken when they say that we can adopt trade and industrial policies without considering our trading partners. They are greatly mistaken, Mr. Speaker, when they say that we can adopt discriminatory laws, regulations and practices against the products, services and capital of our trading partners.
You konw, Mr. Speaker, according to an old law of physics, for every action, there is a reaction. This same law applies to international trade. If a country imposes barriers on other countries' exports, it will have barriers imposed on it. If a country is prepared to negotiate freer entry of goods and
June 28, 1988

sevices from other countries, it will get the same treatment for its own goods and services. Action, reaction!
The so-called nationalists will one day have to realize the interdependence not only of Canada but of all the major industrialized countries.
It is fine to talk about national self-assertation, Mr. Speaker, as long as one can see beyond a narrow parochial view.
Mr. Speaker, to deal with the real world, we need global attitudes and especially a worldwide vision.
To take up our place in the world, Mr. Speaker, we need a world-class industrial structure. What does the Official Opposition propose to ensure the competitiveness of our businesses and industries? They want to resurrect a department which they dismantled as they propose to tear up the Agreement, if they can. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, they want to create a new department or resurrect one which they cut into pieces just six or seven years ago. They want to hire hundreds of public servants to look after international trade and industrial development. They want to spend more than 100 million dollars on God knows what bureaucratic initiatives to accomplish God knows what.
In other words, this proposal is typical of the liberal Party: when faced with a national challenge we see the federal public service, skyrochet, new allocation of funds and greater government interference in everybody's lives. We are all too familiar with the results of such an approach. Look at what happened between 1970 and 1984. The national debt incressed exponentially. And in spite of theire so-called national policies and their speeches on the famous third option, our reliance on the American market increased from 65% or so to more than 75%. That is what they call diversifying our export markets, Mr. Speaker. That is what I call blundering!
One need not look any further, Mr. Speaker, to get an idea of the Liberal party's economic expertise. We only have to look at how they manage their own funds. The key to economic growth and prosperity is not a bigger Canadian Government. The key to industrial productivity and international com-petitivity will not be found in the drawers of the bureaucracy. The key to our economic future lies in the entrepreneurship, the inventiveness and the initiative of our entrepreneurs and workers.
However, they need open and secure access to a world scale market in order to compete around the world. It would be extremely difficult over the next few years for our firms, our industries and our workers to compete with the Japanese, the Europeans and the Americans without a privileged access to the richest and most dynamic market in the world. This, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what we secured through the Free Trade Agreement.
Canada-U.S. Free trade Agreement

Some say that we should rely exclusively on the multilateral trade negotiations under the GATT. They think we are too small, too weak, and not sharp enough to negotiate one on one with the Americans. That is simply a contradiction in terms. Just imagine, if we cannot negotiate with the Americans, how can we hope to negotiate with the European Community and other powerful trading partners such as Japan?
Others insist that the free trade agreement threatens our sovereignty. These are the same people who insist that we negotiate trade liberalization exclusively through the GATT. What they do not say is that each time we introduce a new policy, law or regulation related to international trade, we must ensure that it is consistent with the provisions of the GATT.

Mr. Speaker, does that mean we are any less sovereign? Definitely not! Does that mean we cannot maintain, much less improve our health and welfare programs? Not at all! Does that mean we cannot maintain or improve our regional industrial expansion programs? Definitely not! Are our cultural programs threatened? No, Mr. Speaker, our cultural programs are not threatened. The same goes for our trade agreement with the United States.
Since that Agreement was signed by the Prime Minister and the President last January, we have announced a number of new initiatives in all those areas. For example, Mr. Speaker, our national policy on film distribution and production, our new Copyright Act, our national policy on daycare, our new policy on women subject to marital abuse, our very recent agreement with Quebec on the St. Lawrence River clean-up and the development of fringe areas. Whether it be culture, welfare, health or economic and industrial development, Mr. Speaker, we are totally free and sovereign.
The FT A does not say anything about economic or political union. Mr. Speaker, it is simply a matter of creating a free trade zone as defined under GATT. Canada and the United States will indeed continue to have different policies, different laws, and different regulations. Mr. Speaker, the day the FTA comes into force there will not be any more snow in the Keys than there are palm trees in Chicoutimi.
However, one thing for sure, Mr. Speaker, is that there will be more jobs and more wealth in Canada, the kind of wealth which will enable us to maintain existing programs and introduce new ones. All independent research organizations are at one on this, including the Economic Council, the Conference Board, and Informetrica, just to name a few. To those who are concerned over the issue of sovereignty, Mr. Speaker, I say that political sovereignty without economic clout is nothing more than a mirage. All regions of Canada will benefit from the many free trade spinoffs. Industrialized regions will have freer and more secure access to the American market, and less industrialized regions will finally have an opportunity to diversify their local economy.

June 28, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free trade Agreement
So what is at stake as far as Quebec is concerned, Mr. Speaker? In 1986, Quebec exports were estimated at roughly $21 billion-$3,500 for each man, woman and child in the province-or to put it another way, Mr. Speaker, $14,000 for a family of four. Perhaps you are wondering how much of that the American market accounted for? For about 76 cents of each dollar earned through Quebec exports, Mr. Speaker.
That is why we say that the Free Trade Agreement is the key to our economic future. That is also why the Premier of Quebec is one of the staunchest supporters of free trade. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, when some people tried to use Clause 6 in the Bill to sow discord, the Government of Quebec responded by annoucing that it would take whatever measures are necessary to ensure that provincial acts and regulations are in accordance with the Agreement's provisions.
The Government of Quebec fully understands what is at stake and knows that Quebec industries such as the newsprint industry, the automotive industry and those involved in the production of aluminium, telecommunications equipment, softwood lumber, railway and transport equipment or high tech equipment such as semi-conductors, all need access to the American market not only to grow but to survive.
Given the size and complexity of our country and our interdependence with the world's largest markets, not only the U.S. but also the European community and the growing markets of the Pacific Rim, our horizons must be large and our vision must be global. We simply cannot afford to withdraw into a protectionist shell. More important, as journalist Richard Gwynn has written, free trade represents "the ultimate declaration by Canadians of self-confidence in themselves, confidence both in their ability to compete and their ability to continue as a distinct political and social unit.

Mr. Speaker, in this age of advanced technology and integrate world economy, we need free and secure access to the world's markets. Trough the Free Trade Agreement, we will have unfettered access to the world's richest and most dynamic market.
As the economist Rodrigue Tremblay has said, and I quote:
The United States and Canada have an historic opportunity to go foward in
the direction of economic progress and to help North America become the
most prosperous territory in the world.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I will vote in favour of the historic Free Trade Agreement and the bill to implement it.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this Bill I am concerned that it will, in 20 minutes, be very difficult to explain comprehensively what is wrong with the Bill. I will try to define certain aspects of it which may help the people who are watching understand some of the implications of it.
Canada-U.S. Free trade Agreement
As I talk to people in my riding and other ridings I am continually asked what the trade Bill is all about. People say that they do not understand it, that people are not explaining it to them, that some are saying it is good for Canada, others are saying it is not good for Canada, and they are left out in the cold.
The process which took place with this agreement has left people asking why the Government was rushing to get it signed when we did not have the text. The committee held hearings without knowing the specifics. When a government attempts to do that without allowing full discussion and debate, it is clear that there is fear. There is no question in my mind that the Government has been operating under an intense amount of fear. It has put legislation before this House which comes from a base of nothing but fear.
The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) said that we have to pass this Bill because one form which U.S. protectionism can take is politically inspired distortion of trade remedy law and another form is direct limitation of trade as proposed in earlier versions of the U.S. omnibus trade Bill. We know that the trade Bill did have implications which certainly would make trading very difficult for Canada. We also know that protectionism exists in the United States because its economy is in such a dreadful state. The United States has a dreadful deficit in trade not only with Canada but with Japan and the European Common Market as well.
I heard the Minister say recently that our horizon must be large and our vision global. If we are looking for large horizons and a global vision, we are certainly not looking at a North American fortress. Yet that is exactly what I hear from the government side of the House. I keep hearing the word "harmonize" from each speaker. If you look up "harmonize" in the dictionary you will see that it says "become more like, become similar". That is certainly not what we on this side of the House want.
Over the years Canada has built up a very special value system and a very special country. Our ancestors sacrificed a lot to ensure that trade above the 49th parallel was able to create a society which had its own integrity and which did not become totally dependent. The wars which we fought in 1776 and 1812, and the declaration of our independence in 1867 were all statements that we as a people can be a little bit different but can be strong. We have had great success in doing that.
I heard my colleague from Algoma talking about supply management and the Government saying it was protected. My understanding is that Article 7(10) of the agreement says that both the United States and Canada are protected by Article 11 of the GATT. I agree with that. However, it does not go on to say that there has been a constant move by the Reagan administration and the Canadian delegation to remove Article 11 from the GATT rules. The Government is, on the one hand, saying that we are protecting our supply management system by Section 7(10) of the Accord and, at the same time, is

June 28, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free trade Agreement
moving to remove the clause in the GATT which gives us that protection. That is the most devious kind of hypocrisy that I can think of. I do not think that all the Members on the government side have looked at the agreement in detail and recognized that that kind of thing is happening.
I question whether the Minister for International Trade is as committed to this as he seems when he says that he has not read it. He seems to form a policy with his friends through jokes rather than serious thought. When asked to make a concentrated response about the deal, rather than any serious analysis we see witticism that attempts to put people down.
What will be the implications of this Accord on women? There are those who say there will be wonderful benefits for women. They will only be wonderful for women who are presidents of multinational corporations, because multinational corporations do not want to be restricted by borders.
I am concerned about women in the service and manufacturing sectors, and women in the labour force who perform minimum wage and lower paid jobs. I cannot believe that members of the Government who have seriously considered this legislation believe the deal will help those people. We have known for some time that the United States wants a trade agreement in order to reduce barriers to services. We also know that Brazil and India, along with Canada, have strongly opposed that until now.
Now we find that services are included in the trade agreement. Our concern about services does not refer to hairdressers moving from one community to another, as has been suggested, but the future of data processing, health and education services and the variety of jobs that are being created today. Eighty-two per cent of our economy is in the service sector, and most of those jobs are the better paying jobs held by women. Yet the Government has gone ahead to trade the service sector.
Currently, information in the data processing industry must be collected in the branch plant or at the company where that information is being collected. Many of those jobs exist in Canada. According to a study conducted by the Computer Association of Canada, over 180,000 jobs in data processing will be gone when companies are no longer required to collect that information here. That is the consequence of part of the trade agreement in terms of trade in services. It is important that we consider those details.
The Minister who just spoke talked about all the studies that had recommended this trade agreement as a way to increase the employment base for Canada. The Economic Council of Canada admitted that it did not look at any studies that included the service base. The Macdonald Commission, which rationalized many reasons to support free trade, did not take into account one study on the service industry.
Last night I met some women from the National Organization of Women in the United States, as well as some of the executive from the Feminist Majority. They were very concerned about what could happen to our population in light of all we have worked for over the years. They do not have income security programs, minimum wage requirements or the same working conditions for women for which we have worked so hard.
They were impressed by our ability to have a national old age pension in spite of our small population. Many of those living in poverty in Canada are women over 65 years of age. The women whom I met were amazed at our ability to have developed our social programs over the years. It was with some pride that I acknowledged that we have a reasonably good social network system, particularly for women. It is frightening to realize that all of these programs could be at risk. I become very worried when I hear that this trade agreement means we have confidence in ourselves. If we have confidence in ourselves, we do not have to run in a corner and decide there is only one partner we can trade with and we have to get into an agreement with them. If we have confidence in ourselves, we can stand up proud and tall, believing that Canadian workers can deliver anywhere in the world. We can get into a multinational kind of trade agreement. We do not have to get tied into American foreign policy. We do not have to get tied into every multinational that wants to exploit our people and resources. What we do understand is that our environment is sacred. There is dignity to the work our people do and they should have, and do have in most cases, a quality of life commensurate with the dignity of work they perform. It seems to me that if we are just going to get into the economic constitution of President Reagan, that is not what the majority of Canadians want. It is not what the majority of women in this country want and it certainly is not the future we want to build for our children. I think we understand that very clearly.
I have been very concerned about the fact that not many members on the government side have taken the Accord particularly seriously because, I believe, they trusted some of their cabinet Ministers had read the agreement. If those Members could convince me that this agreement would build a stronger Canadian economy, giving us the kind of sovereignty we had in the past, giving us the ability to have some direction over our own lives, to protect our environment and ensure our native people do not get caught into the whole economic development of our North that could very easily result in a further industrial militarization of our North, if they could convince me that that is what we were going to have, then I would say, yes, we would support it.
I think every one of those things are at risk now. The financial institutions can now come to Canada and purchase any part of the Canadian economy they choose. Can we go down there and set up our banks in the United States? No, we cannot.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating second reading of Bill C-130. Its purpose is to approve the Government's comprehensive trade agreement with the United States.
Should this House and should the Canadian people approve this agreement? Let us take a look at the deal that was made. Let us ask ourselves a basic and simple question. Is it a good deal for Canada? There are two ways to find an answer to this question, two ways to assess it. One is to look at the objective the Government set for itself when it began the negotiations and see whether or not it was achieved in the deal that was concluded. The other is to identify the benefits and the costs of the deal and to see to what extent the benefits, if any, will outweigh these costs.
What was the Government's primary objective in seeking a comprehensive trade deal with the United States? It was to ensure secure access to the American market. This secure access, the Government said, would be achieved by complete exemption for Canada from United States trade remedy laws. This would mean that Canadian exports would no longer be hit by American anti-dumping or countervail duties.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated this primary objective of his Government very clearly and categorically in
June 28, 1988

an interview with The Wall Street Journal in April, 1987, when he said: "Trade remedy laws cannot apply to Canada period..."
Was this objective achieved in the deal covered by Bill C-130? Clearly not. Even with the Government's trade deal Canada's exports will continue to be subject to all current American anti-dumping and countervail laws. In fact, the deal also states that Canadian exports will be subject to any new American trade laws adopted before January 1, 1989. Even though President Reagan vetoed the omnibus congressional trade Bill, if another version is passed that he accepts or if his veto is overridden, then it will apply to Canadian exports to the United States in spite of the Government's trade deal.
Therefore everything remains the same. We are not exempted from U.S. trade remedy laws. They do apply to Canada, in spite of the Prime Minister's words, which are shown to be empty and meaningless, as has happened all too often in the past. However, there is one difference, one change brought about by his deal. There will be a new dispute settlement mechanism. What does this mechanism do? How does it work? What will it accomplish? It comes into effect only at the very end of the presently existing and very lengthy process provided for by the American trade remedy laws now on the books.
The process that has sometimes troubled Canadian exporters remains the same, except in effect it has been lengthened and will have added to it this dispute settlement mechanism which involves the setting up of a panel. However, this panel can decide only if the American law has been correctly applied in terms of its own language. The panel will not have the power to decide whether the American law itself conflicts with the international trade rules created by the GATT, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and therefore could be rejected as being contrary to those GATT rules. This will not be able to be done by the provisions of the Prime Minister's trade deal.
A key issue when it comes to secure access to the American market is the definition of a subsidy. What government payments, what government programs should be considered as a subsidy of the kind that should be subject to countervailing duties to American trade penalties? Under the Prime Minister's trade deal this question, this key issue is left completely open. It is to be negotiated between Canada and the United States for a period of five years and even up to seven years. We are left in total uncertainty as to what the situation will be at the end of this seven-year period.
How will subsidy be defined as a result of these negotiations? What leverage will Canada have at the end of seven years from now to reject American demands that its definitions be accepted, even if these demands mean that Canada's social programs, medical care, pensions, industrial and regional development programs will be considered to be unacceptable subsidies? How can business in Canada make
Canada-U.S. Free trade Agreement
plans for investment and production with this uncertainty hanging over it?
Clearly, the Government did not achieve its primary objective of secure access to the American market in the deal it negotiated with the United States. Let us take a look at the deal in terms of its benefits and its costs.
One benefit supposedly coming from this deal is the elimination of all tariffs, all customs duties on goods moving between our two countries over a period of 10 years. However, 80 per cent to 85 per cent of all goods moving between the United States and Canada already do so duty free. This has been accomplished through the periodic rounds of international trade negotiations under the GATT since the Second World War. The average level of the remaining tariffs has been reduced from some 40 per cent to some 10 per cent.
Surely, even further substantial reductions in tariffs and customs duties would have been achieved through the new round of international tariff negotiations presently under way without the necessity of the massive concessions, the massive costs to Canadian sovereignty, and the massive risks to the economic well-being of this country that have been created by this deal. The Government's claim that the trade deal would bring tremendous benefits to Canadians as consumers through the elimination of customs duties on goods brought into Canada from the United States on examination is just another Conservative Government sham.
If the deal is implemented Canadians will not be able to rush over to the United States on January 1, 1989, and bring back anything they want free of duty. They cannot do this in spite of the suggestions raised by the Government that this will be possible. Instead, what they will buy will still be subject to federal and provincial sales taxes. Customs duties will still be payable if the goods are not manufactured largely in the United States. I am not sure that people realize that many of the consumer goods, the clothing, the appliances that they would like to buy when they see them on sale in the United States are in fact not manufactured in that country. Again, I say that this trade deal is a gigantic sham when it comes to consumer benefits.
What about jobs? The Government originally claimed there would be substantial economic benefits, that large numbers of jobs would result from its trade deal with the United States. Its own Economic Council is showing how wrong these claims are. Before the deal was concluded, the Council predicted
350.000	net new jobs would be created if a deal were entered into. After it looked at the deal that was actually negotiated, the Council revised its estimates sharply downward. It said the elimination of tariffs would create only 76,000 net new jobs over 10 years. Then it said that, if one could assume a threefold increase in productivity-and it did not say exactly how and why Canada would achieve this-the number of jobs created by the deal would be 250,000. This is quite a reduction from the 350,000 originally estimated, and it amounts to only
25.000	net new jobs a year over 10 years.

June 28, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free trade Agreement
This is within the normal margin of error for economic forecasting. Therefore, this degree of net new job creation is very small and could easily happen as a result of the operation of normal domestic fiscal and monetary policy without having the trade deal of the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in place.
If the benefits of the deal are so slight, can it be said that at least the cost of it for Canadians is not high? Unfortunately, this is not the case. The price for Canadians far outweighs any benefits. In brief, that price is a severe limitation on the right of Canadians to make decisions about and policies for the direction of their country through their governments, both federal and provincial.
The policy areas covered by this deal include energy, investment, regional development, industrial policy, agriculture, financial services, and cultural industries.
Let us look at what this deal means, if it goes through, when it comes to energy. If the deal is constitutionally valid, a province would no longer be able to offer a preferential price for its energy to encourage industrial development in that province. The federal Government will no longer be able to ensure that, in times of world energy shortage or crisis, Canada is supplied first, that Canada's needs are taken care of first with its own energy. Instead, under the Government's trade deal, the United States will be entitled to the same proportional share it received from Canada before there was such an energy crisis.
When it comes to investment the deal further reduces, and in some ways wipes out forever, the ability of the federal Government to screen or review American takeovers and to set performance requirements as a condition of their acceptance.
The Government claims over and over that cultural industries are exempt from the deal. It says that is what is stated in clause 2005. However, the very next subclause of 2005 makes clear that if the United States does not like any new Canadian cultural policies or programs it can retaliate against those programs or against some other sector in Canada. Some exemption! It is a meaningless exemption, no matter what the words of the deal say.
The Government makes the same claim of exemption from the deal for our social programs: medicare, pensions, and unemployment insurance. How can we be sure of this when the deal leaves open for seven years of negotiation the definition of subsidy. The United States may yet force on Canada a definition of subsidy that includes and puts at risk these crucial and important social programs for Canadians.
The Government promised Canadians that the Auto Pact would not be touched by any trade deal with the United States. It said over and over during the negotiations that the Auto Pact was not on the table. Now that the deal is public, Canadians should ask whether the Government told them the truth. Canadians can judge for themselves. Even though the
Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) has not read the deal, Canadians can do so. They will see that there is a whole chapter in the text of the agreement on the Auto Pact and the auto sector. The Auto Pact has worked well for Canada and the United States. It has brought about a tremendous expansion of production of cars and parts both in Canada and in the United States, and a tremendous increase of jobs in our country, and in our neighbour's country as well.
There are some 150,000 direct jobs in the Canadian auto industry, and many more indirect jobs in related sectors. Contrary to what the Government claimed, the Auto Pact is not a free trade agreement. It is an agreement that manages our trade in cars and parts with the United States and provided safeguards to ensure production of cars and parts and, therefore, jobs in Canada. It says if a North American automobile company did not provide at least 60 per cent Canadian content on cars and parts sold here, full duties would have to be paid on all imports that those companies bring in from the United States.
This deal will eliminate the duties the Government used in the past to enforce compliance with the content safeguards. In fact, it changes those safeguards from a Canadian content rule to only a 50 per cent North American content rule. This means that the North American auto companies still under the Auto Pact would not have to manufacture one car or one auto part in Canada in order to sell their products duty free in this country. This deal rips the guts out of the Auto Pact. It puts at grave risk tens of thousands of jobs that directly and indirectly depend upon the Canadian auto industry. It is a real sell-out of Canada's interest when it comes to the auto industry, a foundation of our economy.
When the Conservative trade deal is fully examined it is clear that its costs, its price for Canadians, far exceed any possible benefit for our country. As a deal it is simply not a good deal for Canada. What we have here is a massive giveaway of Canada's sovereignty and independence. No wonder we call Bill C-130 nothing more than "the sale of Canada Act".
The Prime Minister recognized what this type of deal with the United States would mean when he said, while campaigning for the leadership of his Party in 1983, that the kind of arrangement with the United States contemplated by this deal was an intrusion into our sovereignty, and he would have none of it now or at any other time. Canadians will ask why did he go back on his word in this important matter with so little for Canadians in return.
In effect, this deal brings about a massive change in our Constitution, not by the process provided for in that Constitution, but by an agreement with another country. It is an intrusion into the jurisdiction of the provinces. Most serious of all, it takes away from present and future generations of Canadians many of the rights that they now have to decide through their Governments what kind of country they want.
June 28, 1988

There is a better alternative to this deal, the Liberal alternative set out in documents we have published. I do not have time to go into that alternative in detail, but I do wish to say that it is to expand trade, lower trade barriers with the United States and with the world through negotiations, not only with the United States, but at the same time with many countries in the world using the GATT system. Under the GATT system it is not only Canada and one other country, the United States, 10 times Canada's size, in which much of Canada's economy is controlled. In the GATT we are joined by many other countries to balance the size, the impact, and economic clout of the United States.
Surely we should seek out the markets of the world as well as the markets of the United States and not lock ourselves, as this deal would do, into a new form of continental protectionism. We should have enough confidence in ourselves to reject this continental protectionism and reach out to the world. Surely this approach is better than what the Government's deal is all about. It is not about trade or tariffs, it is not just a trade deal, it is really about our sovereignty and independence. It is about our future. It is about the economic integration of Canada with the United States. If that happens we also face the eventual cultural, social, and political integration of our country with the United States.
Expressing concern about this does not mean any lack of friendship or regard for the United States. On the contrary, it simply means that we believe there is something that we have built here as Canadians that is worth preserving, and much for us yet to do in this country. Basically this agreement binds future generations of Canadians and their Governments to the current Conservative Government's narrow ideological view of Canada. Surely this is contrary to the fundamental principles of democracy. It should be open to future generations to decide what approach to take to energy, regional development, investment, or social policy. They should be able to say what the balance should be between the operation of market forces and the role of governments in the unfolding of their lives, and not have their rights to do this fixed and limited forever by this Conservative trade deal.
Let future generations of Canadians decide on the values that they consider important, for example, whether they want the American approach to medical care in which a Doctor checks your wallet before he checks your pulse.
I say by way of conclusion that because this agreement is such a sell-out of-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I will take a few minutes to address Bill C-205, an Act to protect heritage railway stations. The object of this Bill is self-evident and laudable, the preservation of Canada's heritage railway stations. I would like to compliment the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) for his unceasing efforts to preserve Canada's heritage and, in particular, his initiatives aimed at saving Canada's heritage railway stations. These stations are close to the heart of most Canadians and I am sure that all Members of the House, no matter what their political stripe, support the intent of Bill C-205.
The Hon. Member for Bow River has certainly done more than his share to awaken Canadians to the value of threatened heritage railway stations. Regardless of the ultimate fate of Bill C-205-I certainly hope it passes-by raising consciousness on this issue the Member has made it easier for concerned citizens to organize and take effective steps necessary to save their heritage railway stations. He has helped people to care about these stations and as more and more of them are saved because of his initiative, the thanks we owe him can only grow larger in the future.
Heritage Railway Stations
To return to the Bill, its purpose is to provide effective mechanisms that would allow concerned citizens to make timely objections to the alteration of railway stations of historical or cultural value. That is a very worthy intent of the Bill and I wholeheartedly accept the principle of it. Bill C-205 is similar to Bill C-211, a Private Member's Bill which in 1985 was introduced by the Hon. Member for Bow River. Heritage railway stations are close to the hearts of many Canadians, including Members of Parliament who have often spoken movingly of the need for their preservation. When such stations are destroyed it is a loss for all Canadians, too many of whom have seen their local railway stations disappear. It would be difficult to underestimate the importance of the contribution that railways have made to the Canadian heritage. In all of Canadian history, in all the ways that Canadians have left a mark on the continent, nothing rivals the importance of the construction of our railways.
In Canada, the railways fulfilled a unique role not only because they brought our country into existence but also because they helped shape our fundamental character. Because of Canada's vast size, geography, dependence upon trade and twin needs for settlement and political identity, efficient modes of transportation have been of vital importance to us. Railways have been the very backbone of our nation. Pierre Berton, although we do not always agree with him, was certainly correct from both a psychological as well as a realistic point of view when he called Canada's railways our "national dream".
Our railways' heritage is the legacy of our national dream, and in large measure it is inextricably bound up with our railway stations themselves. These stations were points of departure and arrival for thousands of families as they travelled on odysseys of settlement across our enormous country. They saw the farewells of tens of thousands of Canadian troops who went off to fight in two world wars, and they were the welcoming sight that greeted the boys when they returned to their home towns.
These stations range from humble structures in tiny hamlets to grand edifices like Montreal's, Windsor's or Toronto's union stations. They have been the scenes of millions of journeys undertaken by Canadians of all walks of life and they loom large in the memories of millions of Canadians. The distress of Canadians when these stations are lost or destroyed is completely understandable and Canadians are familiar with the fights that have gone on when sometimes there has been an effort to destroy a railway station. The undying efforts of the Hon. Member for Bow River to preserve our heritage railway stations are to be heartily applauded. Canada has already lost far too many of these stations.
However, there are encouraging signs that at last we are beginning to do better. The Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada knows how important it is to recognize the heritage value of our railway stations. Twenty-four stations have already been declared on the advice of the board to be of national historical or architectural significance. These are the stations that would be afforded protection under Bill C-205.

June 28, 1988
Heritage Railway Stations
The Board first recommended for commemoration stations which express the development of our various railway lines. This is in keeping with the board's mandate to preserve heritage locations of truly national significance.
For example, the stations at Levis, Quebec and Pictou, Nova Scotia represent the Intercontinental Railway Line. The Canadian Pacific Railway is represented by stations in McAdam, New Brunswick and Kensington, Prince Edward Island and at Rothesay, New Brunswick. Miami, Manitoba, commemorates the heritage of the Canadian Northern Line. The fact that these stations and others, such as Union Station in Toronto, have been recognized to be of national significance by no means precludes other stations from consideration in the future. The Historic Sites and Monuments Board receives submissions more or less continually and judges each proposed railway station on its merits in terms of national historic and/or architectural significance. Our early railway stations are an irreplaceable part of our heritage. Bill C-205 makes this point very clearly and I think that all Members of this House would agree with that sentiment.
The best way to save our heritage railway stations is to encourage co-operation among those parties having a stake in their future. We all have a role to play. This Government is working hard to see to it that Canada's heritage railway stations will be preserved in an appropriate and effective manner. At present the mandate for looking after them is divided and uncertain. The Bill before the House does us a service in reminding us of this fact. The Ministries of Transport and Environment, our railways, CN, CP and VIA, and non-governmental heritage organizations are all involved in this issue. We have certainly heard from the heritage organizations with respect to this Bill. In fact, The Heritage Canada Foundation has recently written about the importance of supporting this Bill and indicates that these buildings will not survive for future generations through good intentions alone. Legislation is the only fair and practical means to ensure that these buildings are protected and cared for.
I think it is appropriate that the House of Commons owes the Hon. Member for Bow River a debt of gratitude for introducing Bill C-205, an Act which has the commendable intent of protecting Canada's heritage railway stations. I, and I am sure other Members of the House, strongly support and recommend that Bill C-205 be referred to the appropriate committee for detailed study and then railway stations across our country so important to our lives will be commemorated. They represent a valuable part of our common history and I hope we will have the support to see this Bill come into fruition.

Mr. Speaker, as you might have expected I rise on this occasion. I want to begin by complimenting the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) on his Bill. It is something that he and many others as well as myself have been working on for a number of years. I want to

One of the most important Bills relating to heritage preservation in Canada is now before Parliament. Bill C-205, an Act to protect heritage railway stations-

It is signed by Jacques Dalibard, Executive Director of the Heritage Canada Foundation.
I am only too happy to add my personal support and the support of my caucus to the Bill of the Hon. Member for Bow River. Over these many years of his experience, and my own, we have fought long and hard to preserve these buildings not just as museums but for practical usage. We want to use the buildings as well as recognize their heritage, history and architecture, as the Hon. Member who just spoke mentioned.
Over the last 10 to 15 years, many dozens of railway stations and other historical objects of some significance have been demolished. We recall the instance of the CPR and the famous railway station near downtown Toronto which was demolished. The Railway Transport Committee of the CTC, six or seven years ago, after it received complaints and found out that the railway had simply moved in bulldozers and levelled the station, ordered the CPR to rebuild and restore it to its original state. I must confess that I have not looked into the situation in the last three or four years, so I do not know if the CPR has done that or not. The letter from The Heritage Canada Foundation mentioned these tragedies, and that was a tragedy. I am not sure if it has been corrected or not.
I think my hon. friend's Bill is timely, in fact overdue, and deserves passage in this House by six o'clock today. I want to say on behalf of my Party that we would agree to that, rather than send this to committee, have it go to Committee of the Whole and be given third reading between now and six o'clock.
I want to bring a particular matter to the attention of the House. My colleague from Bow River, who also sits on the Transport Committee, and other colleagues have had to suffer through this from me on more than one occasion. I want to cite a specific example of a building that the local heritage people in Regina have declared a heritage building, the Union Station in downtown Regina.
Since 1970, and that is quite awhile, I have been trying to get all the parties involved, all the actors in the piece, to agree to establish it as a heritage railway station that would not just sit there as a museum needing upkeep but as one that would have practical usage for many more years to come. That station was one of the early examples of the two competing railways having a Union Station and there is a lot of history there. All during the First World War, the 1920s, the 1930s and the Second World War, right up until the time of VIA

Rail, it was maintained and operated. It had a nice restaurant and one or two shops, and it was kept clean. People by the thousands used it every day.
I and many others in my city and in other places have tried to get that station established as a heritage railway station that would also be a multimodal transportation centre. Greyhound Bus Lines, the Saskatchewan provincial bus company, initially the CPR and subsequently VIA Rail, the City of Regina, the Department of Transport, the Canadian Transport Commission, the Province of Saskatchewan and the Government of Canada were involved. The Chamber of Commerce, the Regina Labour Council, the senior citizens' association and the downtown businessmen's association all agreed that this is something we must do. On two or three occasions, the city council unanimously passed a resolution in favour of doing it. It made alterations to the design of the big shopping complex in downtown Regina, the Cornwall Centre, in order to accommodate this multimodal transportation centre with pedestrian crossings, underpasses, the location of Saskatchewan Drive, whatever was required.
It took until February of 1982 before anything happened. Before I say anything more, I want to tell my colleagues opposite, the Hon. Member for Bow River and my friend, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), that I and others from all political persuasions have deliberately and actively kept this issue totally non-political and non-partisan, and it still took until 1982.
I am just as annoyed at the former NDP Government of Saskatchewan as I am at the present Conservative Government of Saskatchewan. In February of 1982, an agreement was finally signed. We got all the actors in the piece together. They signed an agreement to make that building a multimodal transportation centre as well as a heritage building. To be quite honest, blunt and frank, I think the NDP Government goofed all during the 1970s about getting that done. I fault that Government just as much as any other.
Then we lost the election of April, 1982. In June of 1982, the present provincial Government cancelled the bloody agreement. It was incredible. There was unanimity from all Parties, all business, labour, senior citizens and transportation organizations. This is the kind of tragedy to which The Heritage Canada Foundation refers in its most complimentary letter to the Hon. Member for Bow River.
May I put in a plea, Mr. Speaker? I will beg, grovel, snivel, whatever is required. Would the Hon. Member for Bow River and my good friend, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and other Members, particularly those from the Prairies, make representations to the Premier of Saskatchewan? I met with the premier. I met with the former Minister of Highways and Transportation of Saskatchewan. I tried everything I could, and I did not throw out any NDP dogma or ideology. Mr. Speaker, like my Hon. colleague, I received a letter from Heritage Canada, urging me to take part in this debate, and that is one reason why I welcome this opportunity, because I have been very well served by this agency in the past. I also think the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) made an excellent suggestion, and that is why I decided to speak out in public about my interest in protecting heritage railway stations.
This Bill therefore deserves our attention, and I think the Hon. Member is to be commended, but on the other hand, the proposed legislation should be examined very carefully.
Mr. Speaker, I think all Members will agree that in addition to being a reflection of our past, our old railway stations are often representative of an architectural style that is typical of North America. They bear testimony to the expansion of our country and are a heritage that cannot be replaced. The federal Government has hardly any mechanisms for protecting historic buildings other than those that come directly under its jurisdiction, such as federal buildings.
There are hundreds of railway stations in Canada that can be preserved. In fact, there are several in my riding, and this year, the card I send to all my constituents shows a magnificent example, the station in Huntingdon. There are other stations as well, including the stations in Beauharnois, Valleyfield and Bellerive, that ought to be preserved. There are stations that the wrecker's ball has already destroyed such as Ville de Lery and Ormstown.
Mr. Speaker, the historical role of these stations should not be forgotten, and in fact, they are very much a part of the memories of many Canadians. At a time when railway tracks are disappearing, they are the last vestige of the conquest and settlement of this country. They represent important milestones in the buildings of our railways.
Mr. Speaker, they were the focal point for the departure and arrival of thousands of families on their travels across this vast country they had come to settle. These stations have always brought back memories for those who go back to the places they came from. I imagine many of us in this House have felt the same way. They are part of our national dream.
Many Canadians feel that without historic buildings, a nation loses its sense of history. This heritage must be transmitted from one generation to the next, so that the way of life of a previous generation, how it communicated and how it travelled, and in this case we are talking about the railways, can be understood, and in fact that generation now has a chance to preserve these buildings.

June 28, 1988
Heritage Railway Stations
However, when we hear that despite the joint efforts of municipalities and members of the community, some stations were destroyed, that is a sure sign something must be done to protect them. Earlier, the Hon. Member mentioned a number of cases in his own province, hence the need for measures of the kind proposed by the Hon. Member for Bow River.
In 1976, the Historic Sites and Monuments Board recommended declaring some twenty stations as being of national historic significance. The Minister at the time accepted the Board's recommendation, and in some cases commemorative plaques were put in place. In Quebec, for instance, commemorative plaques were installed at the stations in Levis, Saint-Jean-d'Iberville, Acton Vale, Berthier and at Windsor Station in Montreal. However, this measure was far from adequate, considering the desired goal. In fact, when the Historic Sites and Monuments Board submits recommendations for having certain buildings declared of historical value, this does not put any obligations or constraints on private or public owners. I could mention some examples. In my own riding, in the Municipality of Havelock where a commemorative plaque was installed, a decision was made to preserve the monument that had been so honoured.
The growing awareness of our heritage in recent years shows the good will of all concerned. There are several examples, Mr. Speaker, including Acton Vale. I will make an aside here, because during our caucus meeting to be held in Saint-Hyacinthe this summer, the whole Quebec caucus will take the train from Saint-Hyacinthe to Acton Vale, the very train promised by the Prime Minister in his election campaign, and we will go to this historic station on August 19. So it was possible to preserve this abandoned station in Acton Vale and for it to become a source of pride for the whole community.
If ordinary citizens like the people of Acton Vale can get together to preserve their national heritage, is there any reason why Parliament cannot find an appropriate way to encourage the public in its efforts and to speed up the conservation process considerably? We firmly believe, Mr. Speaker, that a law protecting heritage railway stations is feasible, although complex, and that Bill C-205 is going in the right direction.
The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) was right to present this Bill. Its purpose is to prevent any change that would decrease the value of these stations. It provides that the status of a station may only be changed with the express permission of the Governor in Council, the opinion of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada and the joint recommendation of the Departments of Environment and Transport.
This Bill seems to fill the gap. It would require the railways to ask for specific authorization before demolishing or altering a station. The Governor in Council would have to issue an appropriate decree in each case on the recommendation of both the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Transport and after public hearings by the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the best way to protect heritage railway stations is to encourage cooperation between the railways and people interested in saving these stations. I know that the federal Government is now looking at other options that could be considered for protecting our heritage railway stations.
Mr. Speaker, I would again like to thank the Hon. Member for Bow River for this initiative to protect heritage railway stations in Canada. We are pleased with this initiative and we congratulate the Hon. Member.
We hope that this Bill will be submitted to the appropriate committee so that it can receive all the attention it deserves and be thoroughly considered.

Mr. Taylor: Mr. Speaker, this Bill has already gone through second reading and has been sent to a committee, from which it has not returned. In my view it was sent to the wrong committee, the Committee on Fisheries and Oceans. It has already had tremendous examination. I would certainly like to see it pass. I am receiving letters from all across the country asking that it be passed. I am very much in favour of it going ahead today if at all possible. The Acting Speaker (Mr. Paproski): Is the House ready for the question?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   HERITAGE RAILWAY STATION PROTECTION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   HERITAGE RAILWAY STATION PROTECTION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a further point of order. Would it be in order for me to ask again for unanimous consent for the Bill to go to Committee of the Whole now rather than the legislative committee? If so, I request that unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   HERITAGE RAILWAY STATION PROTECTION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: No. Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. We have been asked that the Bill be directed to a legislative committee for proper examination. We have passed that motion in the House and I would like that to stand. I am not prepared to give unanimous consent.

A motion was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Honourable Deputy to the Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the House went up to the Senate Chamber.
And being returned:
['Agreed.\nAt 5.51 p.m. the sitting of the House was suspended.']

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that when the House went up to the Senate Chamber the Deputy Governor General was pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the Royal Assent to the following Bills:
Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health-Chapter 22.
Bill C-115, an Act to amend the Indian Act (designated lands)-Chapter 23.
Bill C-51, an Act to prohibit the advertising and promotion and respecting the labelling and monitoring of tobacco products-Chapter 20.
Bill C-204, an Act to regulate smoking in the federal workplace and on common carriers and to amend the Hazardous Products Act in relation to cigarette advertising-Chapter 21.
Bill C-l 35, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff (code 9956)-Chapter 24. Bill C-l38, an Act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the Government of Canada for the financial year ending the 31st March, 1989-Chapter 25.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this has been a rather historic day. I think the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) should be congratulated.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
No matter what an individual feels about the piece of legislation, whether opposing or supporting it, she did a tremendous job in getting her Private Members' Bill through. It was a great piece of work and I want to congratulate her on behalf of the Government.
As well, there has been agreement with our colleagues that we have a brief recess until six o'clock, at which time we will resume the free trade debate on Bill C-l30.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed to suspend the sitting until six o'clock?

Agreed.
At 5.51 p.m. the sitting of the House was suspended.
The House resumed at 6 p.m.
